messages.subject: Lack of robustness
messages.subject_clean: Lack of robustness
messages.body_plain: I don't like to look a gift horse in the mouth, but the last few days have left me feeling very frustrated with Stan. To begin with, I spent over a day -- on a project that is already nearly two weeks over-due -- fighting with a problem that turned out to be caused by issues with Stan's implementation of the CDF for the negative binomial function. So I had to redo my model to avoid use of negative binomial. No sooner had I done that, then I ran into another problem: Stan doesn't handle zero-length vectors correctly. In attempting to work around that problem I ran into yet another bug: using max() in declaring the dimensions of a vector/matrix causes Stan to generate C++ code that fails to compile. I am worn out from fighting with this software right now.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Lack of robustness
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Lack of robustness
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,

Sorry to hear about your frustration. I wish we knew about it earlier: I'm sure one of the devs would have been more than happy to help you out before this point.

The development team is trying hard to balance the want to implement new features and making the existing ones more robust. We prioritize bugs, so we'll address the issues you've created as soon as we can hunt down the cause and fix it properly.

Sorry about the zero-length vectors not working. At some point I had made sure all of the Stan language could handle it properly, but the language has grown a lot and this was also before optimization was available in Stan. I'll try to verify, fix, and prevent this from breaking in the future sometime soon.

Regarding numeric stability: repeatable examples are immensely helpful. Thanks for working through that. Michael had also run into the problem independently. We're concerned with the numeric stability of all our functions, but we don't have enough resources to test every possible value for every function, so when users run into trouble, it's really helpful to know what fails. Sorry you ran into it before we patched it; thanks for identifying the problem.

Stan language parsing, but failing to compile: that's our bad. We'll fix that asap. That should never happen.

Hopefully the next time you're back to using Stan, it'll be more robust to your problems. If you get frustrated, feel free to email sooner rather than later.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
In the generated quantities block, for each new data point that you want to predict:
Draw mixture component index k from a categorical distribution with parameters theta.
Draw random value from the k-th mixture component N(mu[k],sigma[k]).

Regarding the 95%-BCI: i.m.h.o. it is what it is; it's just not a very useful summary of a multimodal distribution.

messages.body_plain: Looks about right what your doing. It's just that you are using mixture component index k for all of the i random flow_pred values. Although this doesn't matter for the marginal distributions of each elements in flow_pred, it will matter for the distribution of combinations of the elements of flow_pred (sums, differences, products, average, etc.). If you want to fix this, just make sure to redraw k for each i-th element of flow_pred.

messages.subject_clean: "one chain always breaks during warmup (before it reaches 10%) because poisson_rng rate parameter is > than 1e+9"
messages.body_plain:
Whuuuu?  A parameter of 1e9???  I suggest you rescale the problem in something closer to natural units (for example, if your counts are in the millions, rescale using an offset multiplier of 1 million.  In general in statistical computing (not just Stan) it’s a good idea for parameters to have order of magnitude 1, not 1e9 or 1e-9.  People aren’t always aware of this because classical linear regressions and glms are scale-free.  But once you have priors, scale matters.  Also straight computational issues.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] "one chain always breaks during warmup (before it reaches 10%) because poisson_rng rate parameter is > than 1e+9"
messages.body_plain:
It is somewhat confusing.  Without generated quantities block it converges nicely.  Mean is 2. The maximum of draws is also in the similar range: 30.  However when I add generated quantities block with neg_binomial_2_log_rng it starts reporting that poisson_rng rate parameter is above 1e+9.  I assume neg_binomial is implemented as poisson-gamma mixture. And this occurs very yealy (<10% in warmup).  My solution to this is to replace generated quantities block with corresponding R code.  However, I am using generated quantities for other problems - only neg_binomial has issues.  I would love to use generated quantities always since it is more transparent.

Thank you,
Linas

messages.body_plain:
Interestingly enough with increasing number of mixture components waic increased while Bayesian p-value of chi square test (http://www.bayesian-inference.com/posteriorpredictivechecks) decreased.  How to explain this?  The trace of some of the parameters of the model and model itself are attached.  Any input is welcome.  The R code to determine p-value is below.
goodness.of.fit.pearson <- function (y, y.new <http://y.new>, mu)
{
#
# Goodness-of-Fit assessment in Bayesian analyses
#
Presidual <- array (NA, dim = c (nrow (y.new <http://y.new>), ncol (y.new <http://y.new>)))
fit <- rep (NA, nrow (y.new <http://y.new>))
fit.new <http://fit.new> <- rep (NA, nrow (y.new <http://y.new>))
for (i in 1 : nrow (y.new <http://y.new>)) {
Presidual [i, ] <- (y - mu [i, ]) / sqrt (mu [i, ])
fit [i] <- sum (Presidual [i, ] ^ 2)
fit.new <http://fit.new> [i] <- sum (((y.new <http://y.new> [i, ] - mu [i, ]) / sqrt (mu [i, ])) ^ 2)
}
mean.Presidual <- rep (NA, length (y))
for (j in 1 : length (y)) {
mean.Presidual [j] <- mean (Presidual [, j])
}

Interestingly enough with increasing number of mixture components waic increased while Bayesian p-value of chi square test (http://www.bayesian-inference.com/posteriorpredictivechecks) got better - changed from .95 to .75.  How to explain this?  The trace of some of the parameters of the model and model itself are attached.  Any input is welcome.  The R code to determine p-value is below.

goodness.of.fit.pearson <- function (y, y.new <http://y.new>, mu)
{
#
# Goodness-of-Fit assessment in Bayesian analyses
#
Presidual <- array (NA, dim = c (nrow (y.new <http://y.new>), ncol (y.new <http://y.new>)))
fit <- rep (NA, nrow (y.new <http://y.new>))
fit.new <http://fit.new> <- rep (NA, nrow (y.new <http://y.new>))
for (i in 1 : nrow (y.new <http://y.new>)) {
Presidual [i, ] <- (y - mu [i, ]) / sqrt (mu [i, ])
fit [i] <- sum (Presidual [i, ] ^ 2)
fit.new <http://fit.new> [i] <- sum (((y.new <http://y.new> [i, ] - mu [i, ]) / sqrt (mu [i, ])) ^ 2)
}
mean.Presidual <- rep (NA, length (y))
for (j in 1 : length (y)) {
mean.Presidual [j] <- mean (Presidual [, j])
}
par (mfrow = c (1, 2))
plot (mean.Presidual, main = "Chi Square",
las = 1, xlab = "Index", ylab = "Mean of Chi Square")
abline (h = 0, lwd = 2, col = "red")
#
# Posterior predictive check
#
lim <- range (log (fit), log (fit.new <http://fit.new>))
plot (log (fit), log (fit.new <http://fit.new>),
main = paste ("Graphical posterior predictive check\n",
"chi square test", sep = ""),
las = 1, xlab = "Chi square for actual data set",
ylab = "Chi square for predicted data set", xlim = lim,
ylim = lim, cex.axis = 0.6)
abline (0, 1, lwd = 2, col = "red")
#
# calculate Bayesian p-value
#
mean (fit.new <http://fit.new> > fit) #Bayesian p-value
}

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Ben!  Great suggestion, I'll try to implement it.

On Thursday, April 30, 2015 at 12:53:31 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, April 29, 2015 at 10:25:15 PM UTC-4, Rick Farouni wrote:
> > Correct me if I am wrong but since Factor analysis is mainly a dimensionality reduction technique, the n x p  loading matrix L will have n larger than p, so the rank of L is at most p, (when L has full column rank) and the n x n matrix LL' would have the same rank of L and  so isn't positive definite. That is , if we consider L*L' as a covariance matrix, then it would be rank deficient and won't have a Cholesky factor.  As for A=B*C, I was referring to this rank decomposition  result <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%E2%80%93Penrose_pseudoinverse#Rank_decomposition>.
>
> If the reduced matrix is L * L', then its Cholesky factor is L conceptually. Nevertheless, Stan can't numerically distinguish between rank deficient and indefinite, so cholesky_decompose() would throw an exception.
>
> BTW, if you are thinking of the model as EFA with the factors integrated out, you can use the likelihood that R uses:
>
> > stats:::factanal.fit.mle
> function (cmat, factors, start = NULL, lower = 0.005, control = NULL,
>     ...)
> {
>     FAout <- function(Psi, S, q) {
>         sc <- diag(1/sqrt(Psi))
>         Sstar <- sc %*% S %*% sc
>         E <- eigen(Sstar, symmetric = TRUE)
>         L <- E$vectors[, 1L:q, drop = FALSE]
>         load <- L %*% diag(sqrt(pmax(E$values[1L:q] - 1, 0)),
>             q)
>         diag(sqrt(Psi)) %*% load
>     }
>     FAfn <- function(Psi, S, q) {
>         sc <- diag(1/sqrt(Psi))
>         Sstar <- sc %*% S %*% sc
>         E <- eigen(Sstar, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)
>         e <- E$values[-(1L:q)]
>         e <- sum(log(e) - e) - q + nrow(S)
>         -e
>     }
> ...
>
> That FAfn() function returns the log likelihood so you can express priors on the uniquenesses and not worry about the unidentified loadings. However, it assumes S is a correlation matrix, which makes more sense when doing maximum likelihood (which is invariant) than MCMC.
>
> Ben
>

messages.body_plain:
Scale by adding an constant offset to your linear predictor. To follow Andrews example of scaling by a million: add ln(1e6) to eta as you feed it into neg_binomial_2_log. I don't think it will help prevent the sum of ln(1e6) and eta from reaching 1e9, but at least the values of the model parameters underlying linear predictor eta won't be so ridiculously large.

messages.subject: Re: Parameters that are the bounded sum of other parameters
messages.subject_clean: Parameters that are the bounded sum of other parameters
messages.body_plain:
Another way to think about this would be as a hierarchical model: each condition gets its own alpha parameter, which is drawn from a population alpha_mu and alpha_sigma. This could be used to create shrinkage between the alphas for each condition, and the difference scores between the samples would equate to the offsets (i.e. credible differences between conditions).

What I'm unsure about with that approach is that the next stage of this model will include effects for different people (i.e., I have a within-subjects / repeated measures design). That is, there would eventually be an alpha parameter for each [subject, condition]. In this case, I'm unsure how to build the hyperparameters to provide shrinkage both across conditions and across subjects.

On Friday, May 1, 2015 at 11:30:13 PM UTC+2, Tom Wallis wrote:
> Hi Stan Users Group,
>
> Apologies if this type of question has been covered directly elsewhere; I have looked through relevant posts here <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/JI6yrSZz_Xg/-MGIHytSCSMJ>, here <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/xv-Yjpb7faw/O9cydg8NI8sJ> and here <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/Ur7YPqUoUYM/0uYWTdeIRpUJ> and also the manual under problematic posteriors. I've tried a few things but I'm still struggling to solve my problem.
>
> I am trying to fit a three parameter nonlinear function to some data. I want to estimate how each of these parameters changes across a number of experimental conditions. To do this I thought to use a design matrix composed of sum-to-zero contrasts (created using Python equiv of r's contr.sum()). The beta weights of this design matrix are the offsets to the parameters caused by the conditions, and the intercept is the average parameter value across all the data.
>
> The problem comes in because the three parameters for the main model have bounds: specifically, all must be positive, and one also has an upper bound.
>
> Example: parameter alpha is bounded between 0 and 5 (these constraints are determined by the problem setting). Here's a sketch of the relevant model components for alpha:
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0, upper=5> alpha;
>   vector<lower=-5, upper=5>[D-1] alpha_offsets_raw;
>
> ...
>
>
> transformed parameters {
>     vector<lower=-3, upper=3>[D] alpha_offsets;
>     # constrain offsets to sum to zero:
>     for (i in 1:(D-1)) {
>         alpha_offsets[i] <- alpha_offsets_raw[i];
>     }
>     alpha_offsets[D] <- -sum(alpha_offsets_raw);
> ...
>
> model {
>     alpha ~ normal(3, 1);
>     alpha_offsets_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
>
>     ...
>
>     # loop over data rows:
>     for (i in 1:N) {
>         real this_alpha;
>         this_alpha <- alpha + dot_product(X[i], alpha_offsets);
>         ...
>         y[i] ~ some_function(z[i], this_alpha, ...)
> }
>
> X is a design matrix (actually, N vectors of length D) of sum-to-zero (orthogonal) contrasts with the intercept column *removed* (because I add the intercept, alpha, manually). D is the number of coefficients in the design matrix and N are the observations (rows).
>
> In this model, this_alpha is not constrained to be between 0 and 5 even though alpha is. I would like this_alpha to also follow the constraint.
>
> Some ideas:
>
> min / maxing the value of this_alpha to fall within 0 and 5 would achieve what I'm after, but won't play nice with gradients, as the manual warns.
> I thought maybe I could treat this_alpha as a linear predictor, passing it through the inv_logit function (multiplied by 5) to get a value bounded in the right range. I can see two problems with this: one, it adds an additional nonlinearity that makes the alpha and alpha_offsets parameters a bit hard to interpret and two, I'm not sure how to apply this to my other parameters (which have a lower bound of zero but no upper bounds – I suppose I could add some).
> Fitting all parameters on a log scale would solve the "must be positive" constraint, but again would require more gymnastics on parameter interpretation. Ideally I could have interpretable parameters on alpha and its offsets.
> Any suggestions on a good way to parameterise this model would be much appreciated.
>
> Thanks
>
> Tom

and 1e9 is too large to sample reliably in the headroom of

No, it's just coded directly as a density.  The

everything to 64-bit computation on the inside of Stan.
That's something we need to do longer-term anyway, but
it's probably not going to happen any time soon.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Parameters that are the bounded sum of other parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Parameters that are the bounded sum of other parameters
messages.body_plain:
The sum-to-zero constraint looks right, and I'm afraid the
only general way to proceed is your second suggestion, which
manually rescales the variables.  That's because you have a
dependency on parameters.

The problem is how to use these parameters and a fixed (centered) data
matrix X:

>   real<lower=0, upper=5> alpha;
>   vector<lower=-5, upper=5>[D-1] alpha_offsets_raw;

to make sure this_alpha is in (0,5):

>         this_alpha <- alpha + dot_product(X[i], alpha_offsets);

You can't really do it directly.  One approach would be to
use a scaled inv_logit as you suggest:

   this_alpha <- 5 * inv_logit(alpha + X[i] * alpha_offsets);

You can just declare X to be an array of row vectors or a matrix
and this product will work as written.

Given that you're not applying a prior directory to this_alpha,
you won't need a Jacobian correction for anything.  It's just
like logistic regression, only you don't use this_alpha as
a parameter for a Bernoulli.

- Bob

> On May 2, 2015, at 7:20 AM, Tom Wallis <tsaw...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Another way to think about this would be as a hierarchical model: each condition gets its own alpha parameter, which is drawn from a population alpha_mu and alpha_sigma. This could be used to create shrinkage between the alphas for each condition, and the difference scores between the samples would equate to the offsets (i.e. credible differences between conditions).
>
> What I'm unsure about with that approach is that the next stage of this model will include effects for different people (i.e., I have a within-subjects / repeated measures design). That is, there would eventually be an alpha parameter for each [subject, condition]. In this case, I'm unsure how to build the hyperparameters to provide shrinkage both across conditions and across subjects.
>
> On Friday, May 1, 2015 at 11:30:13 PM UTC+2, Tom Wallis wrote:
> Hi Stan Users Group,
>
> Apologies if this type of question has been covered directly elsewhere; I have looked through relevant posts here, here and here and also the manual under problematic posteriors. I've tried a few things but I'm still struggling to solve my problem.
>
> I am trying to fit a three parameter nonlinear function to some data. I want to estimate how each of these parameters changes across a number of experimental conditions. To do this I thought to use a design matrix composed of sum-to-zero contrasts (created using Python equiv of r's contr.sum()). The beta weights of this design matrix are the offsets to the parameters caused by the conditions, and the intercept is the average parameter value across all the data.
>
> The problem comes in because the three parameters for the main model have bounds: specifically, all must be positive, and one also has an upper bound.
>
> Example: parameter alpha is bounded between 0 and 5 (these constraints are determined by the problem setting). Here's a sketch of the relevant model components for alpha:
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0, upper=5> alpha;
>   vector<lower=-5, upper=5>[D-1] alpha_offsets_raw;
>
> ...
>
>
> transformed parameters {
>     vector<lower=-3, upper=3>[D] alpha_offsets;
>     # constrain offsets to sum to zero:
>     for (i in 1:(D-1)) {
>         alpha_offsets[i] <- alpha_offsets_raw[i];
>     }
>     alpha_offsets[D] <- -sum(alpha_offsets_raw);
> ...
>
> model {
>     alpha ~ normal(3, 1);
>     alpha_offsets_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
>
>     ...
>
>     # loop over data rows:
>     for (i in 1:N) {
>         real this_alpha;
>         this_alpha <- alpha + dot_product(X[i], alpha_offsets);
>         ...
>         y[i] ~ some_function(z[i], this_alpha, ...)
> }
>
> X is a design matrix (actually, N vectors of length D) of sum-to-zero (orthogonal) contrasts with the intercept column *removed* (because I add the intercept, alpha, manually). D is the number of coefficients in the design matrix and N are the observations (rows).
>
> In this model, this_alpha is not constrained to be between 0 and 5 even though alpha is. I would like this_alpha to also follow the constraint.
>
> Some ideas:
>
> 	• min / maxing the value of this_alpha to fall within 0 and 5 would achieve what I'm after, but won't play nice with gradients, as the manual warns.
> 	• I thought maybe I could treat this_alpha as a linear predictor, passing it through the inv_logit function (multiplied by 5) to get a value bounded in the right range. I can see two problems with this: one, it adds an additional nonlinearity that makes the alpha and alpha_offsets parameters a bit hard to interpret and two, I'm not sure how to apply this to my other parameters (which have a lower bound of zero but no upper bounds – I suppose I could add some).
> 	• Fitting all parameters on a log scale would solve the "must be positive" constraint, but again would require more gymnastics on parameter interpretation. Ideally I could have interpretable parameters on alpha and its offsets.
> Any suggestions on a good way to parameterise this model would be much appreciated.
>
> Thanks
>
> Tom

On 3 May 2015 6:36 am, "Bob Carpenter" <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> The sum-to-zero constraint looks right, and I'm afraid the
> only general way to proceed is your second suggestion, which
> manually rescales the variables.  That's because you have a
> dependency on parameters.
>
> The problem is how to use these parameters and a fixed (centered) data
> matrix X:
>
> >   real<lower=0, upper=5> alpha;
> >   vector<lower=-5, upper=5>[D-1] alpha_offsets_raw;
>
> to make sure this_alpha is in (0,5):
>
> >         this_alpha <- alpha + dot_product(X[i], alpha_offsets);
>
>
> You can't really do it directly.  One approach would be to
> use a scaled inv_logit as you suggest:
>
>    this_alpha <- 5 * inv_logit(alpha + X[i] * alpha_offsets);
>
> You can just declare X to be an array of row vectors or a matrix
> and this product will work as written.
>
> Given that you're not applying a prior directory to this_alpha,
> you won't need a Jacobian correction for anything.  It's just
> like logistic regression, only you don't use this_alpha as
> a parameter for a Bernoulli.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On May 2, 2015, at 7:20 AM, Tom Wallis <tsaw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Another way to think about this would be as a hierarchical model: each condition gets its own alpha parameter, which is drawn from a population alpha_mu and alpha_sigma. This could be used to create shrinkage between the alphas for each condition, and the difference scores between the samples would equate to the offsets (i.e. credible differences between conditions).
> >
> > What I'm unsure about with that approach is that the next stage of this model will include effects for different people (i.e., I have a within-subjects / repeated measures design). That is, there would eventually be an alpha parameter for each [subject, condition]. In this case, I'm unsure how to build the hyperparameters to provide shrinkage both across conditions and across subjects.
> >
> > On Friday, May 1, 2015 at 11:30:13 PM UTC+2, Tom Wallis wrote:
> > Hi Stan Users Group,
> >
> > Apologies if this type of question has been covered directly elsewhere; I have looked through relevant posts here, here and here and also the manual under problematic posteriors. I've tried a few things but I'm still struggling to solve my problem.
> >
> > I am trying to fit a three parameter nonlinear function to some data. I want to estimate how each of these parameters changes across a number of experimental conditions. To do this I thought to use a design matrix composed of sum-to-zero contrasts (created using Python equiv of r's contr.sum()). The beta weights of this design matrix are the offsets to the parameters caused by the conditions, and the intercept is the average parameter value across all the data.
> >
> > The problem comes in because the three parameters for the main model have bounds: specifically, all must be positive, and one also has an upper bound.
> >
> > Example: parameter alpha is bounded between 0 and 5 (these constraints are determined by the problem setting). Here's a sketch of the relevant model components for alpha:
> >
> > parameters {
> >   real<lower=0, upper=5> alpha;
> >   vector<lower=-5, upper=5>[D-1] alpha_offsets_raw;
> >
> > ...
> >
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >     vector<lower=-3, upper=3>[D] alpha_offsets;
> >     # constrain offsets to sum to zero:
> >     for (i in 1:(D-1)) {
> >         alpha_offsets[i] <- alpha_offsets_raw[i];
> >     }
> >     alpha_offsets[D] <- -sum(alpha_offsets_raw);
> > ...
> >
> > model {
> >     alpha ~ normal(3, 1);
> >     alpha_offsets_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
> >
> >     ...
> >
> >     # loop over data rows:
> >     for (i in 1:N) {
> >         real this_alpha;
> >         this_alpha <- alpha + dot_product(X[i], alpha_offsets);
> >         ...
> >         y[i] ~ some_function(z[i], this_alpha, ...)
> > }
> >
> > X is a design matrix (actually, N vectors of length D) of sum-to-zero (orthogonal) contrasts with the intercept column *removed* (because I add the intercept, alpha, manually). D is the number of coefficients in the design matrix and N are the observations (rows).
> >
> > In this model, this_alpha is not constrained to be between 0 and 5 even though alpha is. I would like this_alpha to also follow the constraint.
> >
> > Some ideas:
> >
> >       • min / maxing the value of this_alpha to fall within 0 and 5 would achieve what I'm after, but won't play nice with gradients, as the manual warns.
> >       • I thought maybe I could treat this_alpha as a linear predictor, passing it through the inv_logit function (multiplied by 5) to get a value bounded in the right range. I can see two problems with this: one, it adds an additional nonlinearity that makes the alpha and alpha_offsets parameters a bit hard to interpret and two, I'm not sure how to apply this to my other parameters (which have a lower bound of zero but no upper bounds – I suppose I could add some).
> >       • Fitting all parameters on a log scale would solve the "must be positive" constraint, but again would require more gymnastics on parameter interpretation. Ideally I could have interpretable parameters on alpha and its offsets.
> > Any suggestions on a good way to parameterise this model would be much appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "divergent gradient" when log prob and its gradient are both very finite
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] "divergent gradient" when log prob and its gradient are both very finite
messages.body_plain:
> When you say "not robust to large values," do you mean large values of the count, large values of alpha and/or beta, or both?

All three.  Formally problems arise in the current implementation
of the incomplete beta function when alpha is big and/or
when z is close to 1.  Translating to the neg_binomial_2
parameterization this means large alpha, large beta, and/or
large counts.

> Over what range is the current implementation stable (prior to your fix)?

It’s not trivial to specify a stable region in the current implementations
as the convergence of the underlying power series depends on the
interactions of all of the parameters.  Problems can arise in alpha
values as low as 100 if z is sufficiently close to 1 (say z > 0.99) and
it might be even worse.

The fix was checked on a bunch of values pushing into the millions
for z close to zero and one and seemed to be sufficiently accurate
everywhere.

messages.body_plain:
What's going on with:

 vector[Obs] Losses[N];

is that it produces an array of size N whose entries
are vectors of size Obs.  So it's (N x Obs).  Same shape
as this:

  matrix[N,Obs] Losses;

There's a chapter in the manual that goes over differences
between arrays and vectors/row-vectors.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi—to get posterior predictive you’ll want to do this in generated quantities.  If you want a new group, you can define a_rep and y_rep and then, in generated quantities, generate a_rep first and then y_rep.  I’d also recommend stronger priors in your model, something more like N(0,1) or Cauchy(0,1) rather than scales of 10 or 100.  Just make sure your model is scaled appropriately (i.e, that x is of order 1 and that y is not an extremely rare event) and that should be fine.
A

messages.body_plain:
If you used the simplex as a parameter and didn't use softmax to transform, there would be a uniform prior over simplexes and you wouldn't have a problem. The issue is that you're taking a positive_ordered parameter and using a softmax to create a simplex. The posterior over a positive_ordered parameter, without anything else in the model, is improper.

messages.body_plain:
Hi -

I'm working on a 2-stage model with related outcomes, and the same individuals in each level.

The outcome of interest for Level 1 is a continuous diagnostic measure meant to indicate whether an individual is infected with a disease. In this level, I'm estimating a bimodal mixture model with an infected and uninfected group. Level 2 is a survival model of the possibly right-censored time at which the individual actually becomes sick with the disease, given demographics and the diagnostic information. The main thing I'm interested in from this level is the posterior probability of infection for each individual, given demographics and her continuous diagnostic measure, to use as an input to the second level.

I have coded this up, and it works well as a unified model in one stan file, but I'd like to separate the two levels of the model into two separate stan models, so that I can try out alternative specifications for each level. In addition, the current code is hard to maintain, and it would be nice to make it a bit more modular.

I know that one approach would be to just take the posterior mean/median for each individual from stage 1 and use this as a data input stage to the second stage, which I have done successfully before. But this would sacrifice some of the information on variability in the individual diagnoses, which was one of the features I like about the combined model. To be completely hoenst, I'm not sure that this information makes an enormous amount of difference in the eventual outcome, but it seems more correct to me to leave it in than out.

Any thoughts/suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks!

-Jon

messages.body_plain:
This topic of using a posterior from one model as a prior for
another model seems to be trending on stan-users.

There's no easy way to do this directly in Stan.   It's not
coherent statistically to just take the samples from the first model
and plug them into the second model because there is typically "feedback"
from the second model to the first.  The naive pasting together would
produce the same behavior as cut in BUGS.  This is mainly why we haven't
done it and wouldn't recommend it compared to just fitting the joint
model.

(The other area people ask for this is when they trust the first model
more than second model and really do want cut-like behavior, as in
PK/PD models where they know the PK component very well but know the PD
component is misspecified --- they don't want the inferences on the PD
model bleeding back into the PK estimates.)

- Bob

I understand the feedback argument, but isn't this also arguing that priors are also not coherent
statistically?  Right now in Stan I can run one analysis, get a posterior for some parameter "theta",
pick an parametric distribution that approximates the histogram of the samples and use that
as a prior for my next analysis.  This is supposed to be one of the key advantages of Bayes---carrying
over information from one experiment to another.

joint model but also easier to do model-checking as weird knock-on effects don't get to operate.

Hi Folks,

Thanks for all the responses! I think I'm going to stick with the two independent models for the purpose of development and then put them together and do full Bayes on the combined model. Thanks!

One possible mechanical solution I've thought of for exactly this kind of problem would be to write a front-end for R that could use templating (i.e. using brew or something along those lines) to chain together two stan models, taking care to decorate any duplicated variable names, etc. The ideal implementation would look like starting up two rstan runs with their respective input data, i.e. one for each stage, but sampling from the correct posterior by doing all the gnarly C++-style name-mangling in both the R and stan code under the hood. But of course that seems like a lot of work...

Also, this might not be quite the right thread for this, but all of this talk of combined models brings up the question for me of whether to model group-level parameters (in this case a hierarchical model w/about 80 groups) for each level within the same covariance matrix or whether each level should have a separate one. My intuition is that it's ok to put them all together, but wasn't completely sure.

-Jon

I'm very new to GP and had some difficulties in following this from the manual:

In ref manual v2.6.2, Ch 14.4 Predictive Inference with a Gaussian Process -> Analytical Form of Joint Predictive Inference (pg 144):

In the same code regarding omega (copied from Github):
for (i in 1:N2)
   for (j in 1:N2)
     Omega[i,j] <- exp(-pow(x2[i] - x2[j],2))
      + if_else(i==j, 0.1, 0.0);

Questions:

- Ch2 of RW (GP for machine learning) seems to suggest that the noise term is needed for K(X,X) (which I assume translate to Sigma as per Stan manual) only to take care of noisy observations.
- Similar in Andrew's book (pg. 503, 3rd edition), sigma^2 is "added" to K(x,x) only.

2. It seems that the sample code is built for fixed covar function. But, I'm looking at a situation where I first have to fit the GP with training data and then do prediction with test data. In this case, would I still need to add the noise term to omega (which is done in the generated quantities block)?

Many thanks,
Andy

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] incorporating posterior distributions from one model into another
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] incorporating posterior distributions from one model into another
messages.body_plain:
> On May 5, 2015, at 3:40 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Tuesday, May 5, 2015 at 2:51:20 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> This topic of using a posterior from one model as a prior for
> another model seems to be trending on stan-users.
>
> There's no easy way to do this directly in Stan.   It's not
> coherent statistically to just take the samples from the first model
> and plug them into the second model because there is typically "feedback"
> from the second model to the first.
>
> I understand the feedback argument, but isn't this also arguing that priors are also not coherent
> statistically?  Right now in Stan I can run one analysis, get a posterior for some parameter "theta",
> pick an parametric distribution that approximates the histogram of the samples and use that
> as a prior for my next analysis.  This is supposed to be one of the key advantages of Bayes---carrying
> over information from one experiment to another.

Absolutely.  And it works out analytically with the case of a stream of
data and conjugate priors.  The key is that conjugate priors can be viewed
as data.

In other situations, you're only left with the draws from the posterior
of stage 1, which aren't enough to properly formulate a prior for
stage 2.  As you say, you can approximate the prior with a parametric
family, but we don't have any direct mechanism of feeding in the draws
from a previous run to act as a prior to the next run.

It's also problematic when the variables aren't neat sequential priors.

> I think this applies both to multi-stage analyses and to PK/PD style models.  It is more limited than a
> joint model but also easier to do model-checking as weird knock-on effects don't get to operate.

What are "knock-on effects"?

The situation in PK/PD is one where you have a PK model

  p(theta_PK, y_PK, x_PK)

and a PD model conditioned on the PK parameters

  p(theta_PD, y_PD, x_PD | theta_PK)

What the PK/PD modelers want to do is fix the posterior for theta_PK
based only on PK data and priors alpha.  If you were to model
everything jointly,

  p(theta_PK, theta_PD, y_PK, y_PD, x_PK, x_PD)

the PD data and model model would affect the estimates for theta_PK.
That is, the theta_PK isn't a prior for theta_PD with y_PD and x_PD just
being more of the same kind of PK data.

At least I think that's what's going on!

- Bob

> family, but we don't have any direct mechanism of feeding in the draws
> from a previous run to act as a prior to the next run.

I posted my original response because I think the situation where you can approximate the posterior draws with a normal
distribution is pretty common.  If you want to hedge your bets about whether the prior is reasonable you can even weaken
your posterior by using a t-distribution with moderate degrees of freedom or inflate the variance you originally estimated.
For more complex posteriors a mixture of normals, or a mixture of gammas could work as well.  In any case, there's a
common problem and a workable solution and I'm not sure why it doesn't get recommended more often.

> It's also problematic when the variables aren't neat sequential priors.
>
> > I think this applies both to multi-stage analyses and to PK/PD style models.  It is more limited than a
> > joint model but also easier to do model-checking as weird knock-on effects don't get to operate.

>

>
>   p(theta_PK, y_PK, x_PK)
>
> and a PD model conditioned on the PK parameters
>
>   p(theta_PD, y_PD, x_PD | theta_PK)
>
> What the PK/PD modelers want to do is fix the posterior for theta_PK
> based only on PK data and priors alpha.  If you were to model
> everything jointly,
>
>   p(theta_PK, theta_PD, y_PK, y_PD, x_PK, x_PD)
>
> the PD data and model model would affect the estimates for theta_PK.

That's what I called a knock-on effect, I claim ESL as my excuse for weird english.  In this case
I would say the following is fine:

1) use p(theta_PK, y_PK, x_PK) to generate a posterior sample of theta_PK
2) approximate that posterior with a parametric family
3) use the approximate posterior distribution as a fixed prior for the PD model.

> That is, the theta_PK isn't a prior for theta_PD with y_PD and x_PD just
> being more of the same kind of PK data.

I don't think this scenario is any different from any other two-stage analysis, why
would the implications be different just because the second stage is for a different analysis?

Krzysztof

messages.body_plain:
> I posted my original response because I think the situation where you can approximate the posterior draws with a normal
> distribution is pretty common.  If you want to hedge your bets about whether the prior is reasonable you can even weaken
> your posterior by using a t-distribution with moderate degrees of freedom or inflate the variance you originally estimated.
> For more complex posteriors a mixture of normals, or a mixture of gammas could work as well.  In any case, there's a
> common problem and a workable solution and I'm not sure why it doesn't get recommended more often.

Because these simple parametric forms are _terrible_ at capturing the nonlinear
correlations common to realistic posterior distributions.  Besides if these functional
forms were so good we’d just be fitting them to the data (a la variational bays or
expectation propagation) and then doing all of our expectations analytically.
There’s a reason why a huge chunk of the statistical community is studying
Sequential Monte Carlo and not just fitting functional forms.

> On Wednesday, May 6, 2015 at 2:12:20 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On May 5, 2015, at 3:40 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> [snip]
> > There's no easy way to do this directly in Stan.   It's not
> > coherent statistically to just take the samples from the first model
> > and plug them into the second model because there is typically "feedback"
> > from the second model to the first.
> >
> > I understand the feedback argument, but isn't this also arguing that priors are also not coherent
> > statistically?  Right now in Stan I can run one analysis, get a posterior for some parameter "theta",
> > pick an parametric distribution that approximates the histogram of the samples and use that
> > as a prior for my next analysis.  This is supposed to be one of the key advantages of Bayes---carrying
> > over information from one experiment to another.
>
> Absolutely.  And it works out analytically with the case of a stream of
> data and conjugate priors.  The key is that conjugate priors can be viewed
> as data.
>
> In other situations, you're only left with the draws from the posterior
> of stage 1, which aren't enough to properly formulate a prior for
> stage 2.  As you say, you can approximate the prior with a parametric
> family, but we don't have any direct mechanism of feeding in the draws
> from a previous run to act as a prior to the next run.
>
>
> I posted my original response because I think the situation where you can approximate the posterior draws with a normal
> distribution is pretty common.  If you want to hedge your bets about whether the prior is reasonable you can even weaken
> your posterior by using a t-distribution with moderate degrees of freedom or inflate the variance you originally estimated.
> For more complex posteriors a mixture of normals, or a mixture of gammas could work as well.  In any case, there's a
> common problem and a workable solution and I'm not sure why it doesn't get recommended more often.
>
>
> It's also problematic when the variables aren't neat sequential priors.
>
> > I think this applies both to multi-stage analyses and to PK/PD style models.  It is more limited than a
> > joint model but also easier to do model-checking as weird knock-on effects don't get to operate.
>
> What are "knock-on effects"?
>
>
>
>
> The situation in PK/PD is one where you have a PK model
>
>   p(theta_PK, y_PK, x_PK)
>
> and a PD model conditioned on the PK parameters
>
>   p(theta_PD, y_PD, x_PD | theta_PK)
>
> What the PK/PD modelers want to do is fix the posterior for theta_PK
> based only on PK data and priors alpha.  If you were to model
> everything jointly,
>
>   p(theta_PK, theta_PD, y_PK, y_PD, x_PK, x_PD)
>
> the PD data and model model would affect the estimates for theta_PK.
>
> That's what I called a knock-on effect, I claim ESL as my excuse for weird english.  In this case
> I would say the following is fine:
>
> 1) use p(theta_PK, y_PK, x_PK) to generate a posterior sample of theta_PK
> 2) approximate that posterior with a parametric family
> 3) use the approximate posterior distribution as a fixed prior for the PD model.
>
> That is, the theta_PK isn't a prior for theta_PD with y_PD and x_PD just
> being more of the same kind of PK data.
>
> I don't think this scenario is any different from any other two-stage analysis, why
> would the implications be different just because the second stage is for a different analysis?

In this PK/PD setting, they explicitly *don't* want it to be a typical
two-stage analysis.  In the typical two stager you get:

  Stage 1:  prior(1) -> data(1) -> posterior(1)

  Stage 2: posterior(1) -> data(2) -> posterior(2)

and now posterior(2) won't match posterior(1).  But what you want with
cut is to *fix* posterior(1) and not let data(2) update it.

Instead, that posterior(1) isn't a prior for data(2), but another joint
parameter, and they don't want data(2) messing with, it so they can't just
make posterior(1) a parameter in the Stage 2 program.

- Bob

> > I posted my original response because I think the situation where you can approximate the posterior draws with a normal
> > distribution is pretty common.  If you want to hedge your bets about whether the prior is reasonable you can even weaken
> > your posterior by using a t-distribution with moderate degrees of freedom or inflate the variance you originally estimated.
> > For more complex posteriors a mixture of normals, or a mixture of gammas could work as well.  In any case, there's a
> > common problem and a workable solution and I'm not sure why it doesn't get recommended more often.
>
> Because these simple parametric forms are _terrible_ at capturing the nonlinear
> correlations common to realistic posterior distributions.

But we do advocate weak priors even though those are also terrible at capturing correlations.  My point is
that the boundary is as clear as your answer makes it out to be.  If I notice that my
posterior is banana-shaped, I can come up with an informative banana-shaped parametric form
for my posterior. If on the other hand, I miss that sort of multiplicative identifiability problem,
I might specify harmless-seeming weak priors that really impact my analysis.  In either case the
only way you find out is by examining the posterior samples (if you're lucky) or the functional
form of the posterior.

> Besides if these functional
> forms were so good we’d just be fitting them to the data (a la variational bays or
> expectation propagation) and then doing all of our expectations analytically.
> There’s a reason why a huge chunk of the statistical community is studying
> Sequential Monte Carlo and not just fitting functional forms.

Fair enough, I can see that it's a preferable approach.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question on noise term in the Gaussian Process code in the manual
messages.body_plain:
We had some discussion off-list (insights below are due to Aki) and here's a summary for posterity...

1. The manual doesn't match GPML or BDA, so we're going to fix that. Here's what it'll say:

for (i in 1:N2)
    for (j in 1:N2)

      Omega[i,j] <- exp(-pow(x2[i] - x2[j],2));

Note that if you wanted the posterior distribution over y, rather than the latent function f, you would want to do it the way it's done currently in the manual, with an extra variance 0.1 on the main diagonal. But usually you're interested in posterior inference about f, so there's no need for that extra term.

2. Question: Why are length-scales sometimes parameterized as rho^2 and sometimes as l^2, where rho^2 =1/l^2?
Answer: Choosing l^2 is better for interpretation's sake because then it's in the same units as x (well, l is in the same units...) Both should be constrained to be positive (lower=0), and in terms of sampling both are log-transformed with log(rho^2)=-log(l^2), so they should be equivalent with respect to sampling efficiency.

Seth

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question on noise term in the Gaussian Process code in the manual
messages.body_plain:
> 1. The manual doesn't match GPML or BDA, so we're going to fix that. Here's what it'll say:
>
> for (i in 1:N2)
>     for (j in 1:N2)
>       Omega[i,j] <- exp(-pow(x2[i] - x2[j],2));
>
> Note that if you wanted the posterior distribution over y, rather than the latent function f, you would want to do it the way it's done currently in the manual, with an extra variance 0.1 on the main diagonal. But usually you're interested in posterior inference about f, so there's no need for that extra term.

Careful — the GP prior is often assumed to not have a diagonal component but
there’s no reason why it can’t.  Even when using the GP to model some prior
directly it can be useful to add a diagonal term.

> 2. Question: Why are length-scales sometimes parameterized as rho^2 and sometimes as l^2, where rho^2 =1/l^2?
> Answer: Choosing l^2 is better for interpretation's sake because then it's in the same units as x (well, l is in the same units...) Both should be constrained to be positive (lower=0), and in terms of sampling both are log-transformed with log(rho^2)=-log(l^2), so they should be equivalent with respect to sampling efficiency.

Again, this can be a subtle issue.  In particular, when we start using nontrivial
priors the two parameterizations will yield different posteriors*.  In other words,
the sampling performance can be different because the priors can will be
different.  When thinking about length scales the l parameterization is more
interpretable and hence leads to better prior specification, and when thinking
about ARD the rho parameterization is more interpretable and head leads
to better prior specifications.

* Fun fact: cauchy(x) = cauchy(1/x) so the Half-Cauchy priors would actually
yield the same posterior in either case.

>
> Seth

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] further confusion
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] further confusion
messages.body_plain:
We can add abs() and max() to do what you want.  Historically,
I just went with what C++ used for the functions.

The issue is signatures.  int will be promoted to real if necessary but
not the other way around.

For abs, we now have:

  int abs(int);
  real abs(real);

  real fabs(real);

This means you get

  abs(1)   : int
  abs(1.0) : real

  fabs(1)   : real
  fabs(1.0) : real

And for max, it's

  int max(int, int);

  real fmax(real, real);

which gives you:

  max(1, 2) : int

  max(1.0, 2)    ILLEGAL
  max(2, 1.0)    ILLEGAL
  max(1.0, 2.0)  ILLEGAL

  fmax(1, 2)     : real
  fmax(1.0, 2)   : real
  fmax(1, 2.0)   : real
  fmax(1.0, 2.0) : real

I take it what you're asking for is

  * those illegal ones to be defined to be real

  * fabs and fmax to just go away (be deprecated, then removed)

This is all trivial (which means a day at least of coding, testing,
changing the manuals, and ideally trawling through existing examples).
We just need to decide to do it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] matrix or array of integers?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] matrix or array of integers?
messages.body_plain:
For a 2D array of integers, that's:

  int y[I,J];

But you can't use it in matrix operations.  If you want
to do that you need to have

  matrix[I,J] y;

But then you can't use it on the LHS of binomial or bernoulli.
If you need the binomial or bernoulli, then you are going to
need to convert the int array to a matrix in the transformed
data block.

  transformed data {
    matrix[I,J] y_mat;

    y_mat <- to_matrix(y);
  }

It's more efficient defining it once as transformed data than to
reconvert it using to_matrix() each time you need it.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Key concept is the five basic types of Stan:

  real-valued:
    real, vector, row_vector, matrix

  integer-valued:
    int

Then you can have an array of any dimensionality of
any basic type.

So when you declare y as

  int y[I,J];

you get a 2D integer array.

So assuming you want this:

...

  for (i in 1:I)
    for (j in 1:J)
      y[i,j] ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);

for a fixed theta, you can do this:

  to_array_1d(y) ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);

They go in column-major order (or last-index order
if the argument is more than 2D).  And then theta
has to be either a single real value or an array or
vector of I*J real values.

- Bob

data {
  int J;                         // #people in y
  int T;                         // #time points in y

  int K_phi;                     // #parameters in phi
  matrix[J,T] y;
  vector[T] x;
  vector[K_phi] mu_phi_g;        // pseudo-prior mean
  cov_matrix[K_phi] Sigma_phi_g; // pseudo-prior variance
}
parameters {
  matrix[J,K] eta_a;
  real<lower=0> sigma_y;
  vector[K] mu_a;
  vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_a;    // Now assuming indep
  real b;                        // Shared parameter
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[J,K] a;
  vector[K_phi] phi;

  for (j in 1:J)

    for (k in 1:K)
      a[j,k] <- mu_a[k] + sigma_a[k]*eta_a[j,k];
  phi[1] <- mu_a[1];
  phi[2] <- mu_a[2];
  phi[3] <- b;
  phi[4] <- log(sigma_a[1]);
  phi[5] <- log(sigma_a[2]);
  phi[6] <- log(sigma_y);
}
model {
  matrix[J,T] y_pred;

  for (j in 1:J)

    for (t in 1:T)
      y_pred[j,t] <- a[j,1] + a[j,2]*x[t] + b*x[t]^2;
  to_vector(y) ~ normal(to_vector(y_pred), sigma_y);
  to_vector(eta_a) ~ normal(0,1);
  phi ~ multi_normal(mu_phi_g, Sigma_phi_g);
}

You don’t really have to worry about phi here; I just included it to remind you of my desire to be able to access the concatenated transformed parameter vector directly (I need to do this because I’m running an EP-like algorithm).

And from your previous message it looks like I need to change to_vector to to_array_1d.  But then I have a horrible feeling that the indexes will get flipped.

So maybe the best solution is to change my model and make “a” and “y_pred” into 2-way arrays instead of matrices?

This array/matrix thing is always tripping me up!

Intuitively, I want to update the posterior of \theta_i sequentially as the series_i goes on. Is it possible to do this in Stan? Thank you.

Best,
Ziyuan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks -

I have two-part question about using the multivariate gaussian process functions in stan. I hunted around for some examples and couldn't find any, so I thought I'd put this out here. The first is a general modeling question about when it is appropriate to use this approach and the second is a simple implementation question using multi_gp in stan (pg 387 of the stan 2.6 guide).

Modeling question: I have a spatial dataset of age-specific disease prevalence data. The data are each associated with a health care center in a large city. I want to model spatial variation in the age-prevalence relationship, using a GP based on the distances between health centers for spatial smoothing. In addition, there are spatially varying treatment effects that I want to include in the model as well. So, my model has 3 parameters: intercept, slope for age and the treatment effect. I expect all of these to vary similarly in space, so that neighborhoods with a similar intercept should definitely have a similar age effect and likely similar treatment effects. My question is, is this a situation in which it is ok/advisable to use a single kernel matrix to model all three of these coefficients, or at least the two that I'm sure should vary together?  Also, if I'm including the noise term on the diagonal of the kernel matrix, is it OK to not include an unstructured random effect term for each of these?

My implementation question related to how to specify the kernel matrix and vector of inverse scale parameters to sample all of these coefficients at once. My plan is to use the typical approach for a squared-exponential covariance function, allowing for noise on the diagonal. The inverse scales will be specified by a vector of length three, with the first element (representing the intercept) constrained to 1, so that the fitted noise term represents the unstructured variation in the area-level intercepts, and the other terms in the vector of inverse scales control the noise and covariances appropriately for the age & treatment coefficients. Is this correct?

Thanks!

-Jon

There are some densities, like the Cauchy, that don't have
finite mean and variance.  It's unlikely to come up in a posterior
unless you have very fat-tailed priors and very little data.

 - Section 8.4 in Vanhatalo, J., Pietiläinen, V., & Vehtari, A. (2010). Approximate inference for disease mapping with sparse Gaussian processes. Statistics in medicine,29(15), 1580-1607.
and
 - Zhang H. Inconsistent estimation and asymptotically equal interpolations in model-based geostatistics. Journal of the American Statistical
Association 2004; 99(465):250--261.
 - Diggle, P. J., Tawn, J. A., and Moyeed, R. A. (1998). Model-based geostatistics. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series C (Applied Statistics), 47(3):299–350.

This may make the posterior difficult to sample unless good (weakly) informative priors are used.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] gaussian process with multiple outputs
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] gaussian process with multiple outputs
messages.body_plain:
There are a few ways to model correlations in spatial dependence.

Firstly, if you assume that the effects vary spatially with similar
smoothing but not necessarily similar trends (for example, the
effects have the same length scale but they might not all be
positive in the same regions) then you can use a covariance
function with common hyperparameters.  If that’s too restrictive
then you can make the hyperparameters hierarchical across
the sites.

On the other hand if the effects are expected to have similar
smoothing and similar trends then you can consider a
hierarchical GP, for example

y ~ GP(0, X)
y_age ~ GP(y, X)
y_prevalence ~ GP(y, X)

You can even go double hierarchical and have a hierarchical
GP with hierarchical hyperparameters.  Again, it really depends
on what prior relationships you want to encode in the model.

I’m not sure diagonal noise will completely replace random
effects at each site — especially if there may be nonspatially-
corrected effects.  I’d start with just the GP and then add
random effects to see if you get better PPCs.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model involving complex numbers
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical model involving complex numbers
messages.body_plain:
There is not going to be any need for complex differentiation — in fact it
will probably be easier to write out your entire model in terms of the
real-valued components (especially if your likelihood depends on only
the magnitude of the complex numbers).

In any case, you cannot map an N-dimensional distribution into
an (M != N)-dimensional one as probability will not be conserved.
What you have to do is engineer an N->N map and then marginalize.
For example,

p(x, y)
-> p( f(x, y), y) | d (f, y) / d (x, y) | (f, y)
-> \int dy p( f, y) | d (f, y) / d (x, y) | (f, y)

messages.body_plain:
One possible solution is to use multi-output covariance functions (review article of the subject: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.6251). The basic idea is quite simple: say we have outputs X and Y, then we would jointly model them with a single GP, ie.

(X,Y) ~ GP(0, K), where covariance function

K = [b11 * K_xx, b12 * K_xy,
       b21 * K_yx, b22 * K_yy]

and B = [b11, b12; b21, b22] is symmetric positive definite matrix capturing correlations between X and Y. For example, if B is the identity matrix, then they are independent etc. Unfortunately, the computational burden is quite large, this doesn't really scale up nicely. How many health centers there is in the dataset?

too.

It's tricky with covariance matrices, though, because you need
to make sure the result is positive definite or you'll run into
trouble sampling.

Seconding everything Michael and Herra said. Since it can be tricky to
get even simple versions of what you describe working, I'd start as
simple as possible--no spatial model--and build from there. (Maybe
you've already done this?) Certainly email the list with code if you
get stuck.

I have to say that the existence of multi_gp is news to me; are there
examples somewhere of it being used? (It's weird to me that the mean
is fixed at 0...)

The model you're describing is interesting--do I understand correctly
that you have a linear model prevalence = intercept + b1 * age + b2 *
treatment and you want intercept, b1, and b2 to be spatially varying?
I was going to suggest above that you stick with a Gaussian
observation model if possible as that seems to help a lot with speed,
but now I'm not actual clear on what your observation model is, since
the GP is a prior on the coefficients, right? So are you using a
Binomial distribution for the prevalence?

An alternative you might consider if there are non-linearities in the
relationship between age and prevalence is that a GP would also be
appropriate there as well, and you could even do everything in one
model:

f(age, location, treatment) ~ GP(0, K_location * (1 + K_age + K_treatment))

Or more interpretable:

f(age, location, treatment) ~ GP(b0 + b1 * age + b2 * treatment,
K_location * (1 + K_age + K_treatment))

In this model f(.) is the log-prevalence. As noted above a Gaussian
observation model helps a lot with speed, so if you can accept the
approximation, I've had success using a "pseudo-likelihood" approach
with case counts k_i out of a population n_i with \hat p_i =
(k_i+1)/(n_i+2):

k_i/n_i ~ GP(invlogit(b0 + b1 * age_i), K_age + diag(\hat p_i (1-\hat
p_i) / n_i))

Seth

seen is one I originally described — fill in the (M - N) missing
entries with the last (M - N) original parameters.

Hi Everyone -

Thanks for all of the helpful replies! Just to clarify, it's a binomial observation model. For now, I'm sticking with a single kernel matrix and focusing on just a spatially varying intercept and treatment effect and leaving the age effect fixed across units. I did try a version without the spatial smoothing and it was very noisy and PPCs were way off; these are pretty small units, some of which have only a few observations. They're all completely contiguous and form subsets of neighborhoods, so it seems like keeping the spatial info in there is worthwhile, even though it is indeed something of a pain.

The 'treatment' in this case is a household exposure of varying intensity, so the model also includes covariates for household-level attributes; which is a total bummer b/c otherwise the gaussian approximation seems perfect for this purpose!

Just a quick question for future reference on combining GPs with possibly differing dimensionalities: If K_age is a 30 x 30 kernel matrix with its own hyperparameters and K_space is a 100 x 100 matrix with its own hyperparameters, is the covariance between age i and j at locations k and l just the sum of K_age[i,j] and K_space[k,l]? Seems like it, just wanted to be sure.

Thanks!

-Jon

> Seconding everything Michael and Herra said. Since it can be tricky to
> get even simple versions of what you describe working, I'd start as

> you've already done this?) Certainly email the list with code if you
> get stuck.
>

> examples somewhere of it being used? (It's weird to me that the mean
> is fixed at 0...)
>
> The model you're describing is interesting--do I understand correctly
> that you have a linear model prevalence = intercept + b1 * age + b2 *
> treatment and you want intercept, b1, and b2 to be spatially varying?
> I was going to suggest above that you stick with a Gaussian
> observation model if possible as that seems to help a lot with speed,
> but now I'm not actual clear on what your observation model is, since
> the GP is a prior on the coefficients, right? So are you using a
> Binomial distribution for the prevalence?
>
> An alternative you might consider if there are non-linearities in the
> relationship between age and prevalence is that a GP would also be
> appropriate there as well, and you could even do everything in one
> model:
>
> f(age, location, treatment) ~ GP(0, K_location * (1 + K_age + K_treatment))
>
> Or more interpretable:
>
> f(age, location, treatment) ~ GP(b0 + b1 * age + b2 * treatment,
> K_location * (1 + K_age + K_treatment))

> > correlations between X and Y. For example, if B is the identity matrix, then

messages.body_plain:
> so the model also includes covariates for household-level attributes

But can't you put these into the mean function and still use the
Gaussian approximation? e.g.

f(age,location) ~ GP(invlogit(b0 + b1 * age + b2 * location + b3 *
household covariate 1 + b4 * household covariate 2), K)

> is the covariance between age i and j at locations k and l just the sum of K_age[i,j] and K_space[k,l]?

You could try an additive model, which is what you're describing, but
you could also try a multiplicative model instead. The additive model
is equivalent to two separate GPs:

f ~ GP(0, K1 + K2) is equivalent to f ~ GP(0, K1) + GP(0,K2)

But the multiplicative model might be better. Both should eventually
allow for some speedups--I haven't done much with speeding up additive
GP models but maybe someone else has code to share?--though it may
take some changes to core Stan; I'm working on code for the
multiplicative case (using Kronecker products) at the moment, will
hopefully share with the list soon.

Quick caution--if you have a multiplicative model:

k1(x,x') = v1 * exp( - (|x-x'|/l1)^2)
k2(y,y') = v2 * exp( - (|y-y'|/l2)^2)

Then you'll want to get rid of v2 for identifiability:

k1(x,x')*k2(y,y') = v1 * exp( - (|x-x'|/l1)^2) * exp( - (|y-y'|/l2)^2)

Seth

messages.body_plain:
You didn't mention anything about your data or what prior information you have.

I usually scale x to have mean 0 and std 1. Then as a weakly informative prior I would use
 l ~ t(4,0,1)
where l=1/rho is the lengthscale. This prior is quite flat for l<1 and for l>1 the behavior of the GP does not change much (it's already close to linear), so it's unlikely that larger values are needed, but having the thick tail still provides the possibility that the data overrules the prior.

For eta I would use prior which says that eta_sq is likely to be smaller than the total variance of the data.  I usually scale y to have mean 0 and std 1, and thus I can use prior favoring eta<1. Note that, the total variance of the predicted data is eta_sq+sigma_sq, so you could also define a prior on eta_sq+sigma_sq and prior on ratio eta_sq/sigma_sq which is the proportion of the explained variance.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
I’d actually go the other way and think about using the GP to
model the slopes and intercepts as in a GLM.  So, for example,
you have binomial data which you could write in Stan as

y ~ binomial( inv_logit( f(covariates) ) );
y ~ binomial_logit( f(covariates) );

Usually we take f to be linear,

f = X * beta + alpha

with the beta, alpha hierarchical over groups.  But you could
also treat f as GP or just think about modeling beta and alpha
as GPs,

f = X * beta(spatial location) + alpha(spatial location);
alpha ~ GP(0, Sigma(hyperparams));
beta ~ GP(0, Sigma(hyperparams);
// add hyperprior here

And then if you had multiple effects you could do something like

f = X * (beta1(spatial location) + beta2(spatial location))
     + alpha1(spatial location) + alpha2(spatial location);
alpha1 ~ GP(y_alpha, Sigma(hyperparameters);
alpha2 ~ GP(y_alpha, Sigma(hyperparameters);
y_alpha ~ GP(0, Sigma);
// hyper priors
beta1 ~ GP(y_beta, Sigma(hyperparameters);
beta2 ~ GP(y_beta, Sigma(hyperparameters);
y_beta ~ GP(0, Sigma);
// hyper priors

This assumes that the mean effects and the group variations
have the same length scales, but you could easily generalize
this with different hyperparameters or hierarchical hyperparameters,
etc...

On Wednesday, May 13, 2015 at 1:17:14 PM UTC-4, Robert Grant wrote:
> It is a reparameterisation in order to speed up Gibbs, though I find myself wondering "why bother". I probably will play with it at some point, though like you, my to-do list seems to stretch almost to retirement. They haven't published data, but there's nothing special about the application.

This model is not so easy to do in Stan. The Bernoulli / binomial part is pretty standard but they parameterize

log(p) = x' * beta

which requires x * beta < 1, rather than

log(p / (1 - p)) = x' * beta

which allows x * beta to be any real number.

Rejecting draws where x' * beta > 1 makes Stan draw from an invalid posterior because you can't divide by Pr(x' * beta < 1) to normalize it.

I think the way to go about it is to declare

vector<upper=1> eta;

and make the location of the prior distribution for eta[i] be (a function of) x[i]' * beta. But it is not clear how best to do that and even still it does not accomplish the authors' goals of interpreting an element of beta as a risk-ratio.

Ben

> On May 13, 2015, at 7:16 AM, Paula Sarkis <paula.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> This is the first time I use STAN (PyStan) and my first application on MCMC so I am trying to figure how to sample from the posterior distribution.
> I want to fit a straight line to my data points with uncertainties in both the dependent and independent data points.
> The equation of the line is:
>                                              ytrue = alpha + beta * xtrue + epsilon
> where epsilon ~ N(0, sigma), sigma is unknown and treated as a model parameter.
>
> My posterior distribution is
>                                           p(xtrue) * p(x | xtrue) * p(ytrue | alpha, beta, sigma, xtrue ) * p(ytrue | y)
>
> My model is expressed hierarchically:
>
> xtrue ~ mixture of Gaussians with weight: theta, mean: mu, and standard deviation: tau
> ytrue ~ N(alpha + beta *xtrue, sigma)
> x ~ N(xtrue, xerr)
> y ~ N(ytrue, yerr)
>
> Here is my code:
>
> data {
>
>     int<lower=0> N; // number of points
>
>     int<lower=0> K; // number of mixture gaussians
>
>     vector[N] x; // x values
>
>     vector[N] y; // y values
>
>     real xerr; // x uncertainties
>
>     real yerr; // y uncertainties
>
> }
>
>
>
> parameters {
>
>     real alpha; // intercept
>
>     real beta; // slope
>
>     real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation ?! (check if s.d. or variance)
>
>     vector[N] xtrue;
>
>     vector[N] ytrue;
>
>     simplex[K] theta;
>
>     real mu[K];
>
>     real<upper=0> tau[K];
>
> }
>
>
>
> model {
>
>     vector[N] ymodel;
>
>     real logxtrue[K];
>
>
>
>     // PRIORS
>
>     for (k in 1:K) {
>
>     mu[k] ~ normal(0, 10);
>
>     tau[k] ~ uniform(0, 100);
>
>     }
>
>
>
>     for (n in 1:N) {
>
>         for (k in 1:K) {
>
>              logxtrue[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(xtrue[n], mu[k], tau[k]);
>
>          }
>
>     lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(logxtrue);
>
>     }
>
>
>     ymodel <- alpha + beta * xtrue;
>
>     ytrue ~ normal(ymodel, sigma);
>
>
>     x ~ normal(xtrue, xerr);
>
>     y ~ normal(ytrue, yerr);
>
> }
>
> """
>
>
>
>
> Question 1:
> In STAN language, when I define x ~ normal(mean, sigma)
> Is this the standard deviation or the variance?

Variance --- the function part of the manual explains all the
formulas used for probability functions.

> Question 2:
> In my model I wrote the log distribution of xtrue but I wrote the usual normal distribution of ytrue, x, and y. Is this correct? How does STAN interpret normal(mean, sigma)?

  y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

is, roughly speaking modulo constants, translated to

  increment_log_prob(normal_log(y, mu, sigma));

The constants only affect efficiency and the value of lp__ up to a constant.

> My concerns are that mathematically/statistically speaking I should either define my log-likelihood or my likelihood. In the model that I wrote above I used both of them, is this 'STAN-ically' correct?

It's always a log density including both log prior and log likelihood
if you've decomposed your density that way.

> Question 3:
> Given the hierarchical model of my problem above, did I write my model correctly?

No.

First, that's not a hierarchical model in the statistical sense.
It's a mixture model.

But it's not right for a mixture model because of this:

>     real<upper=0> tau[K];

>     tau[k] ~ uniform(0, 100);

Every parameter should have support for every value matching its
declared constraints.  Here the constraint is upper=0, which admits
values of -10, which are out of support.  We don't recommend these
flat bounded priors anyway --- see the regression chapter of the manual
for our current thinking on priors.

But you don't want just lower=0, either.  You either want to
change the prior to not be on a constrained interval (recommended)
or change the constraint to <lower=0, upper=100> to match the support
in the model.

> Question 4:
> I ran the program but got the following error:
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> stan::prob::normal_log: Scale parameter is -0.275754, but must be > 0!
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
> Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
> Rejecting initialization at zero because of vanishing density.
>
>
> Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
>  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
>
> Can someone please explain to me what is this error?

Yes, you have a scale parameter that's negative but it has
to be positive.

You have this:

>     real<upper=0> tau[K];

where you needed <lower=0,upper=100> given that (a) you need it to
be positive, and (b) you needed it to be constrained to (0,100) for
the uniform(0,100).

- Bob

On Wed, May 13, 2015 at 10:29 PM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
> You didn't mention anything about your data or what prior information you have.
>
> I usually scale x to have mean 0 and std 1. Then as a weakly informative prior I would use
>  l ~ t(4,0,1)
> where l=1/rho is the lengthscale. This prior is quite flat for l<1 and for l>1 the behavior of the GP does not change much (it's already close to linear), so it's unlikely that larger values are needed, but having the thick tail still provides the possibility that the data overrules the prior.
>
> For eta I would use prior which says that eta_sq is likely to be smaller than the total variance of the data.  I usually scale y to have mean 0 and std 1, and thus I can use prior favoring eta<1. Note that, the total variance of the predicted data is eta_sq+sigma_sq, so you could also define a prior on eta_sq+sigma_sq and prior on ratio eta_sq/sigma_sq which is the proportion of the explained variance.
>
>
> Aki
>
>

On 05/12, Joshua Rosenau wrote:
> Not sure if this helps, but do note the existence of the ordered and positive_ordered data types, and the ordered_logistic distribution, which you might use instead of the bernoulli_logit. You could use ordered (or positive_ordered) to hold k-1 cutpoints (for a Likert scale with k options), then use ordered_logistic to estimate the cutpoints.
>
> That generates a graded response model, if you estimate the cutpoints separately for each item. If you have only one set of cutpoints, it would be a rating scale model. There’s been a fair bit of list discussion about how to code a GRM lately, which should get you started.
>
> OTOH, if the Likert scale has an obvious division and you don’t care about the finer details (e.g., Strongly Agree, Agree, Don’t know, Disagree, Strongly Disagree; it only matters if someone agrees at all), then it could make sense to collapse the categories and do the simpler bernoulli_logit (but I wouldn’t just cut arbitrarily at the sample average). Doing that does throw out information which might be meaningful in assessing item difficulty or a person’s ability (if, for instance, a more able person is more likely to select the “strongly” version). If the options aren’t inherently ordered (multiple choice, but not Likert) you could either score it and analyze right/wrong using bernoulli_logit, or code it as a GPCM. I haven’t seen that discussed on the list, but should work if you use a vector instead of ordered, and use categorical_logit instead of bernoulli_logit.
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sharing.  We've been meaning to do something like
this ourselves for ages so would like to include a variant of
what you're doing in our doc or example models.

Were you reproducing a textbook example here (I saw the Iris
data)?

Did you fit it with optimization or MCMC?

How well did it work?  We'd like to include an example with
some of the mods suggested below.

Where'd iris come from?  This is the first line of the R:

  iris1=iris[1:100,]

I'd suggest replacing

  fitted_middle[q,n, j] <- 1/ (1+exp(-beta_middle[q, j] * fitted_middle[q-1,n]'));

with:

  fitted_middle[q,n,j] <- inv_logit(beta_middle[q,j] * fitted_middle[q-1,n]');

dot_product's even a bit faster.  It would be even faster to do a matrix
product for beta_middle and fitted_middle and assign to a temporary and then
assign to fitted_middel using inverse logit.

If you define beta_final and fitted_middle appropriately in terms
of shape, you should be able to replace this:

  y_data[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(beta_final' * fitted_middle[num_hidden,n]');

with

  y_data ~ bernoulli_logit(beta_final * fitted_middle);

without having to transform anything (though transforms aren't that
expensive because there are no derivatives).

Also, if you don't want to save all of fitted_middle, you could
declare and define it in the model block as a local variable.

- Bob

I didn't take this example from a textbook but just wanted to get a better understanding of neural networks and rstan so I decided to try it..

Sam

messages.body_plain:
No, with

  value <- exp(value_raw);

If you put it in an if-else, you get a non-differentiable
point at zero rather than nice smooth behavior.

But if you want cutpoints for ordinal logit, then there are
ordered and positive ordered vector types that do it for you.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] It'd be interesting to compare Stan to this BUGS approach for binomial family, log link GLMs.
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] It'd be interesting to compare Stan to this BUGS approach for binomial family, log link GLMs.
messages.body_plain:
A big part of the motivation here is that people don't get odds ratios. Sadly, medics tend to be taught that it is an approximate risk ratio (for historical but stupid reasons) and this results in massive distortions when communicating risk to patients.

I'm also wondering if there is mileage in modelling logits as normal, including an intercept, and monitoring their corresponding risks. For continuous independent variables, you could specify a few points of interest on the scale and assess the risk at each. Or monitor the linear predictor for each observation, and then you can get marginal effects (I think; I haven't really had enough sleep to go making bold statements like that). Fundamentally, I think researchers should be giving readers risks whenever they can, and that is probably more often than ML GLMs allow.

messages.body_plain:
Stan respects standard linear algebra rather than trying
to conform vectors.  So you can't multiply two row vectors.
The reason it does this is because multiplying row vectors
a and b is ambiguous --- if it's a * b', you get a scalar
but if it's a' * b, you get a matrix.

You can use .* for elementwise multiplication, transpose
one or the other to get a scalar or matrix result, or
use the dot_product() function to just take a dot product.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> functional form:
> - my prior expectation is that y should be a linear function with zero intercept of x for  "small values" of x (most of the observations) but is bounded by an unknown asymptote values on both positive and negative ends. The intuition is that y will react to x linearly, but only up to a certain extend. Beyond that, an incremental change would have increasingly small impact on y.

I assume you mean "close to linear" and not "linear". If you assume saturation, you should use some sigmoid function possibly combined with a GP, instead of just GP with a prior mean zero and a stationary covariance function.

> Data size:
> - number of observations(N): typically, 10 - 15
> - number of x(D): can be up to 15

The latest model I found in this thread was t_gp_fp.stan. It has a GP prior with squared exponential covariance function allowing nonlinearities and full interactions. If rho is large for all dimensions, then you have too much flexibility compared to your small N. Since your x's are highly correlated, it would be useful use factor analysis distance (projecting x's to a lower dimensional manifold). Alternatively you need to have a strongly sparsifying prior for rho and hope that only one (or two) dimensions will be used.

 Aki

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am doing some preliminary testing of a model in RStan, and I am getting some puzzling diagnostics. I am wondering if this is a bug, or if I am missing something.

I run a stan model with 2 chains and 200 iterations (just for testing).

If I use print(), the output states (among other things):
"2 chains, each with iter=200; warmup=100; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=100, total post-warmup draws=200."

If I use monitor(), the output states (among other things):
"Inference for the input samples (2 chains: each with iter=100; warmup=50):"

Moreover, n_eff and Rhat differ considerably in the outputs of these two calls.

My impression is that stan actually runs 200 iterations for each of the two chains, and that the monitor-function gets this wrong? Or am I missing something here?

messages.subject: Re: Inconsistent diagnostics in rstan?
messages.subject_clean: Inconsistent diagnostics in rstan?
messages.body_plain:
monitor() by default throws away the first half of whatever array you give it, and as.array() throws away the warmup. So, monitor(as.array(stanfit)) throws away half the post-burnin. Call it with warmup = 0.

Ben
