messages.body_plain:
one alternative way to communicate risk in an intuitively accessible way is to use average predictive comparisons:
www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf>
for logistic regressions they provide an estimate of by how many percentages a risk changes, if a predictor variable changes by one unit.
the one draw back of this method is that it is computationally intensive (i.e. it involves pairwise comparison of predicted outcomes for all pairs of rows in a data set), so that one has to draw a random sample of the data to compute average predictive comparisons if one has large data sets.
guido

messages.subject: survival analysis model with latent variables and discontinuous hazard
messages.subject_clean: survival analysis model with latent variables and discontinuous hazard
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks -

I'm hoping to implement a weibull survival model for some left-censored current-status data where I have the result of a diagnostic test at age a_i telling me whether an individual was infected before that age, but not when.

I'm hoping to model the actual time of infection on the interval from [0,a_i) as a latent variable, using a weibull proportional hazards model. I want to obtain this value to use as input to another model predicting whether an individual develops disease over some time period.

The only issue is that there is a single time-varying covariate for a discrete exposure event occurring over a 1-year period that will shift the hazard up by a constant over this period.

What I'm worried about is that this discontinuity will mess up stan's gradient calculations for the latent infection time and result in very slow optimization. I'm attaching images showing an example PDF and CDF for an individual with only background exposure up to age 9 and then intensified exposure from age 9-10.

One thought I had was to break the calculation into two pieces, treating the latent infection time as a mixture with one component representing the pre-exposure infection times and the other other the post-exposure times. This would result in 2 latent variables, one from [0,A-1) and another from [A-1,A), so that each would have a continuous domain. But I was wondering if there was a simpler approach that might require less in the way of coding gymnastics?

Thanks!

-Jon

I know this would involve a jacobian adjustment, since I want to sample the values of Z*A. So, I wanted to see if I was missing something about using vector-valued constraints and check to see what the appropriate jacobian adjustment would be for the approach I described.

Thanks!

-Jon

No.  Millions of parameters are a lot, or 100s of thousands
in some cases.

- Bob

> On May 15, 2015, at 2:10 AM, Paula Sarkis <paula.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On May 15, 2015 07:40, "Bob Carpenter" <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > The default for theta is uniform, and because theta is a simplex,
> > that's proper.
>
> So I should put/fix a prior on theta.
>
> > 375 data points is not many at all.  You shouldn't need
> > 15K iterations to get reasonable effective sample size.
> >
> I have 373 data points which is equivalent to having 755 parameters in my model to make inference on. (Xtrue (373) + ytrue (373) + alpha. Beta, sigma (3) + K=2 Gaussians (6) which sum up to 755 parameters).
>
> Now my question is 755 parameters considered a lot?

You'll have to quantify what you mean by a lot!

We've fit models with over a million parameters and millions
of data points, but have had more trouble (in terms of speed)
with models with a few thousand parameters and much more complex
structure.

> > P.S.  The model looks like a mixture model with measurement error for x
> > and then another measurement error model for y and a simple
> > regression of y on x.   Not sure what that does all together.
> >
>
> True! That's exactly what I'm trying to do. I'm trying to fit a straight line to my data points with measurement errors on both the dependent and independent parameters.
>
> I'm not next to the laptop now, but basically if I fix my priors should 15000 interactions with 4 chains be enough?

Depends on what you want to do.  You want to look at n_eff, which
is the effective number of samples you have and the se column, which
estimate error on posterior mean estimates.

Usually a few hundred iterations run with four chains are plenty --- it
gets std errors well below posterior std deviation for parameters.  100
effective samples means std errors that are 10% of posterior std deviations.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I use R inside Emacs Org mode for its literate programming and reproducibility capabilities.  That means I use stan() in Org mode, too.

Unfortunately, I can't figure out how to get the output I want.  I create an org code block something like this:

#+NAME: blockname
#+HEADER: :session R:sessionname
#+BEGIN_SRC R :exports both :results value :exports both
<R code to define data>
<R code to call stan()>
print(stanfitobjectname)
#+END_SRC

According to http://orgmode.org/manual/Results-of-evaluation.html, ":results value" in a ":session" should give the last evaluation performed by R (technically the value of .Last.value), which I thought would be the result of the print().  Unfortunately, I get nothing except the "+RESULTS: blockname header.

Changing to ":results output" gives me all the sampling information from stan() plus the output of print().

I am not sure what stan's verbose does, but verbose = FALSE doesn't get rid of the sampling information.

Is there anyone here who might use Org mode and knows how to eliminate the sampling log from the output here while keeping the result of the print()?

If not, does anyone know why the results of print(stanfitobjectname) doesn't seem to end up in .Last.value and what, if anything, I might do about it?

I'd ask on an Org mode channel, but I'm not yet sure how to explain it to them, and I figure the probability is higher here that someone uses Org mode than the probability that someone there uses Stan.  I may be wrong.

Bill

> Stan respects standard linear algebra rather than trying
> to conform vectors.  So you can't multiply two row vectors.
> The reason it does this is because multiplying row vectors
> a and b is ambiguous --- if it's a * b', you get a scalar
> but if it's a' * b, you get a matrix.
>

messages.subject_clean: Howto compile advanced models?
messages.body_plain:
Dear members  of the Stan user list mailing group,

I am quite new to Stan, but have worked a lot with JAGS and WinBUGS. I recently wrote a multilevel (hierarchical) model with repeated measurements that I want to fit in RStan. This model compiles and runs fine when I have a dataset of limited size, but no longer compiles when I use the full dataset. I have a feeling this has something to do with the large amount of missing values: in the larger dataset (about 3000 subjects) I have studies with observations for only one (of the 6) follow-up time points.

Following the instructions of the OpenBUGS example "camel" , I need to specify a parameter for each missing value in the " parameters section" . Since I am not interested in the actual values of the missing values, I am wondering more efficient ways exist to model the missing values. The current setup leads to a huge amout of parameters being estimated and stored in memory, this is not really what I want.

In any case, the model that currently needs to be compiled uses about 41GB of RAM at the time it is aborted. This does not seem right. When I compile the same model with a smaller version of the dataset (only smaller in terms of #subjects, i.e. a total of +-300 subjects out of the +-3000 subjects), it compiles and runs perfectly, and requires about 1GB to 2GB of RAM. The smaller version has about 100 missing values.

Thanks in advance for your help!!

Thomas

I have a feeling this has something to do with the large amount of missing values: in the larger dataset (about 3000 subjects) I have studies with observations for only one (of the 6) follow-up time points.
>
> Following the instructions of the OpenBUGS example "camel" , I need to specify a parameter for each missing value in the " parameters section" . Since I am not interested in the actual values of the missing values, I am wondering more efficient ways exist to model the missing values.

The only other thing you can do is marginalize out the variable.

It's hard to say how to do that exactly without seeing more of your
model.

> The current setup leads to a huge amout of parameters being estimated and stored in memory, this is not really what I want.
>
> In any case, the model that currently needs to be compiled uses about 41GB of RAM at the time it is aborted.

Which version of RStan are you using?

The size Stan needs is based on the expression graph computed by
the model block.  Stan consumes roughly 24 bytes per subexpression plus
8 bytes per operand.

A rough estimate should be about 40 bytes times the number of parameters,
assuming most of the operations are binary.  The density functions are pretty
economical --- they take 16 bytes per operand but only form a single expression.

> This does not seem right. When I compile the same model with a smaller version of the dataset (only smaller in terms of #subjects, i.e. a total of +-300 subjects out of the +-3000 subjects), it compiles and runs perfectly, and requires about 1GB to 2GB of RAM. The smaller version has about 100 missing values.

If it's only 10 times larger in terms of expression graph
it should only take up 10 times as much space.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: pk modeling in stan: one compartmental model with lag
messages.subject_clean: pk modeling in stan: one compartmental model with lag
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Stan does not care to my knowledge about the discontinuity in the derivative - rather the discontinuity in the log-likelihood is a problem. However, if the data is such that Stan will not often try out parameter values which cause these jumps in the log-lik, then it is ok.

I did fit lag time models (in simple PK settings) and I was surprised how well it worked - but I can't recall if I had so much courage to put a random effect on the tlag; probably not.

In short: just try it... otherwise you can always us the transit cmt approach.

Best,
Sebastian

On Friday, May 15, 2015 at 8:37:11 PM UTC+2, Linas Mockus wrote:
> Hi,
>
> Does anybody have experience with modeling a lag?  Technically the first derivative is discontinuous at lag time and the model as it is described in textbooks doesn't converge in stan.
>
> Thanks for any advice,
> Linas

messages.body_plain:
I checked the data you posted. There's not many observations, and it seems to be quite noisy. You mentioned that you assume saturation. I think you should start by fitting sigmoidal function and maybe with Student's t distribution first. It's likely that GP does not provide any improvement over that...

Aki

On Friday, May 15, 2015 at 7:00:35 AM UTC+3, Andy Choi wrote:
> Hi Aki,
>
> Many thanks.
>
> 1. I was meant to say "close to linear".
>
> 2. Yes, that the GP model I'm working right now. In terms of the rho's, will explore the approaches you suggested. But, just thinking out loud, would it work if I assume some kind of multivariate prior over the rho's?
>
>
>
>
>
> On Fri, May 15, 2015 at 3:20 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
> > > functional form:
> > > - my prior expectation is that y should be a linear function with zero intercept of x for  "small values" of x (most of the observations) but is bounded by an unknown asymptote values on both positive and negative ends. The intuition is that y will react to x linearly, but only up to a certain extend. Beyond that, an incremental change would have increasingly small impact on y.
> >
> > I assume you mean "close to linear" and not "linear". If you assume saturation, you should use some sigmoid function possibly combined with a GP, instead of just GP with a prior mean zero and a stationary covariance function.
> >
> > > Data size:
> > > - number of observations(N): typically, 10 - 15
> > > - number of x(D): can be up to 15
> >
> > The latest model I found in this thread was t_gp_fp.stan. It has a GP prior with squared exponential covariance function allowing nonlinearities and full interactions. If rho is large for all dimensions, then you have too much flexibility compared to your small N. Since your x's are highly correlated, it would be useful use factor analysis distance (projecting x's to a lower dimensional manifold). Alternatively you need to have a strongly sparsifying prior for rho and hope that only one (or two) dimensions will be used.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Assigning boundary values in the data block for vectors
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Assigning boundary values in the data block for vectors
messages.body_plain:
The bounds on data are there for error checking and
to help readers of the code understand what you have
in mind for data.  They don't change the fit.

But failing early with a sensible error message is
what you want code to do, so we strongly recommend using
constraints on data wherever possible.

- Bob

:-)  Not to worry.  In case others haven't, it's located at http://orgmode.org/.  It grew out of Emacs' very flexible outline mode.  It offers the ability to include and execute source from multiple languages, sharing output from one as input to another, and it offers flexible publishing capabilities.  In a way, it's an Emacs version of RStudio, except that it came first.  After trying RStudio for a bit and despite liking it, I came back to org mode.

Here is their section on active code in org-mode: http://orgmode.org/worg/org-contrib/babel/index.html.

>
> Is there some control you want on the output of CmdStan
> or Rstan or what?  And when you say print(), you mean the print()
> in Stan's language or from R or where?
>

If you open the .org file I attached, there are #+ header lines at the start that get inserted as standard templates, if you will.

The line starting with a single '*' is a top-level header.

Then the block starting #+NAME: and ending #+END_SRC is a code block with associated headers. BEGIN_SRC R says it's an R code block, and the three lines inside are thus pure R.  The print() is R's command.

Hmm.  One could define Stan as another supported language <http://orgmode.org/worg/org-contrib/babel/languages.html> and then write Stan code directly into an Org code block.  It wouldn't be the first compiled language; you can already see C, C++, Fortran, .....  I don't know if it's worth the effort, though.

I think this is the problem.  http://orgmode.org/manual/Results-of-evaluation.html suggests that .Last.value may not be being set as org-mode expects; http://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Last.value.html tells what that R variable is.

If, using RStudio, I print something in R and then print a stanfit object in R, entering .Last.value after each, I get different results from the two print() commands:

> print('abc')
[1] "abc"
> .Last.value
[1] "abc"
> print(stanobject)
Inference for Stan model: Model01.

NULL

Is it possible that print.stanfit simply forgot to set .Last.value?  Is there a reason it can't be set?

Thanks,

Bill

PS: My current workaround is to split the print() statement into a second code block. I export nothing from the stan() command block, and I export everything from the print() block.  If print.stanfit() can be made to set .Last.value, that would be better.

messages.subject_clean: Improving occupancy model performance
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am building an occupancy model in Stan and am wondering if I am missing any tricks to improve performance. I read through chapter 20 of the manual, but nothing jumped out at me. I've based my model off of examples provided on the group forum that marginalizes out the discrete latent variables (here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/occupancy/stan-users/EpX-wzOj7L4/v6Dgg-QkX9MJ> and here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/occupancy/stan-users/ZuLmNl4Q9xc/OhYbS5V2f6EJ>, thank you Quresh and Bob!).

I am building up to a more complicated model and right now have 3 models. Each builds upon the previous model and is slightly more complicated than the previous model:

Model 1: This model includes a probability of occurrence (psi) and a probability of detection (P). I used the logit functions for stability (and parameters muP and muPsi). I also used a binomial function to vectorize the bernoulli function in the example previously posted and avoid a for loop over the Y matrix (also the real data I eventual plan on analyzing is in this format).
muPsi <-  alpha
muP    <- gamma

Model 2: This model includes a trend, tau, through time acting upon the occurrence.
muPsi[t] <-  alpha + tau (t - 1)
muP    <- gamma

In the the code, I avoid a for loop by using vectors
muPsi <-  alpha + tau * yearLessOne
where
yearLessOne = 0:(nYears - 1)

Model 3: includes model 2 plus a moving average for muPsi
muPsi <-  alpha + tau * yearLessOne + epsilon
where
  epsilon[1] ~ normal(0, sigmaEta);
  for (year in 2:nYears)
    epsilon[year] ~ normal(rho * epsilon[year - 1], sigmaEta);

In this model, rho is not recoverable. Usually all or almost all of the epsilon parameter include 0 in their 80% CrI (see example output). I suspect this why Stan does not recover rho. Does this seem like a reasonable explanation?

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-IAyic2hDtuU/VVtxFZJIKGI/AAAAAAAAATw/jZRUJFbCMkc/s1600/example.jpeg>

I would like make sure my code is optimized for two reasons. First, I am using model 3 to build more complicated model and am having slower convergence with it. Second, my ultimate goal is use multiple (100 or more) "fake data" sets as described in chapter 8 of Gelman and Hill (2007) and compare the model's ability to recover parameters across a range of parameter values.

I have attached 4 files (plus the embedded figure). My R script and the 3 models as Stan files. I am using RStan version 2.6.0 on Windows 7 with R version 3.2.0 (although I don't think that matters). Please let me know if you need anything else.

Richard Erickson

PS Bob, when I get this working, I would be willing to write up examples for the Stan manual.

> to coda format) and apply RStan's R-hat and n_eff routines.
>

With a single chain that is a mcmc object defined in the coda package,

arr <- as.matrix(mcmcobject)
dim(arr) <- c(nrow(arr), 1L, ncol(arr))
library(rstan)
monitor(arr, warmup = 0)

With a mcmc.list object (perhaps produced by as.mcmc), it is conceptually the same thing but the dimensions have to be permuted.

arr <- as.array(mcmclistobject)
arr <- aperm(arr, c(1,3,2))
monitor(arr, warmup = 0)

Ben

quantities.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

I put the question below out on the list and didn't get much traction, and am coming back hat in hand to see if anyone can verify that my solution makes any sense at all.

What I ended up doing, and which seems to recover the right parameters, was to treat the current-status observation of infection for individuals with a postive test (i.e. a positive test, Y = 1, says you were infected at some time before the time of testing, but not when) as a mixture of two latent infection times, one for the period [a,a-1) where a is the individual's current age, and the other from [a-1, a) in which the hazard of infection is known to increase by a constant, which of course introduces a discontinuity into the PDF that I'm concerned will mess up autodiff in stan if I didn't treat this outcome as a mixture.

If f(x) is the full pdf over the range from [0,a), including both the background exposure and the observed period of elevated exposure from [a-1,a), what I did was to calculate the probability of an infection before A as, where F is the integral of f over the specified range:

Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1) = (F(0 < t < a_i-1)*f(t_1) /F(0 < t < a_i-1)) +  (F(a_i-1 < t < a_i)*f(t_12 /F(a_i-1 < t < a_i)),

which simplifies to just:

Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1) = f(t_1) + f(t_2)

This seems to work but I still somehow don't believe it. So I wanted to check and see if you guys thought this was right.

Sorry for any abuse of notation!

Thanks!

-Jon

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: pk modeling in stan: one compartmental model with lag
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

There are pros and cons for any of the choices - this is my opinion: From my experience it is always good (numerical wise) to fit ke; or since we are fitting the logs of it, I prefer to fit 1/ke which is the mean residence time; something I understand much better and can hence give better priors. On the contrary, the allometic weight scaling theory stuff is only applicable to Cl and V. Now, what I tend to do, is fit MRTs and then convert them to Cl, apply allometric scaling to Cl and V to finally calculate the patient specific MRT_j. Handling rates or MRTs is a matter of sign-convention on the log-scale...

In principle, I think, you want random effects on all parameters. It usually a compromise of what you can fit with your data and how willing you are to use informative priors on the omegas (variance components of the random effects). Again, this is also a very specific question which can only be answered in the context of your problem and data.

My last point concerning logs: I always calculate the log of the concentrations, so I tend to use the log_diff_exp() / log_sum_exp() functions very often. If you keep all the computations in log space, then all those products become just sums (should be easier for Stan to deal with). The concentration 0 I then always represent as -25, which is reasonably close to 0 on the natural scale.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jon,

Good to see Stan, uh, spreading among disease ecologists. I'm not sure I follow everything you wrote, but let me give it a try...

Key point: am I correct that, if Y_i = 1, then we know that individual i was infected between 0 and testing time a_i ? (I'll leave off the subscript i's from here on out.)

So you start with a piecewise density function f(t), where t is the infection time you want to infer, 0 < t < a, with pieces f1(t) on [0, a-1) and f2(t) on [a-1,a].

And another part of your model, let's say g(s | t) for some additional parameters/data s, depends on t, in such a way that you can't analytically integrate it out, so you need it to be a latent variable.

You split this into two weighted models, and introduce two mutually exclusive latent infection times t1 and t2, assigned their respective pieces of the probability distribution f1(t1) and f2(t2); properly normalized these would be

f1(t1) = f(t1) / F(0, a-1)
f2(t2) = f(t2) / F(a-1, a)

but for Stan's purposes, provided a is a constant, the normalizations can be left out for a bit of extra speed.

[Side confusion: I don't get your notation Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1). Read literally, that looks to me like, "the probability that t is less than a_i if they tested positive", but I thought testing positive implied t < a_i. Perhaps you meant, Pr(t | Y = 1), where t < a_i — in other words, just the density function f(t)? In which case, well, f(t) = f1(t) + f2(t) by definition, since f1(t) is zero from 0 to a-1 and f2(t) is zero from a-1 to a.]

Seems to me you then just need to carry t1, t2 to define a mixed sub-model g(s | t1, t2), so that

g(s | t1, t2) = F(0, a-1) * g(s | t1) + F(a-1, a) * g(s | t2)

since F(0, a-1) and F(a-1, a) are the prior probabilities for t being in [0, a-1) and [a-1, a], respectively. Does that make sense?

Alternatively, you could replace your discontinuous density function with something that's smoothed out at the boundary, e.g.

f(t) = f1(t) * [1 - h(t)] + f2(t) * h(t)

where h(t) is a smoothed step function (say, a narrow logistic) that rapidly goes from 0 to 1 at (a - 1). And then you have a single well-behaved infection time t.

Ed

On Wednesday, May 20, 2015 at 5:01:47 PM UTC-7, Jon Zelner wrote:
> Hi everyone -
>
> I put the question below out on the list and didn't get much traction, and am coming back hat in hand to see if anyone can verify that my solution makes any sense at all.
>
> What I ended up doing, and which seems to recover the right parameters, was to treat the current-status observation of infection for individuals with a postive test (i.e. a positive test, Y = 1, says you were infected at some time before the time of testing, but not when) as a mixture of two latent infection times, one for the period [a,a-1) where a is the individual's current age, and the other from [a-1, a) in which the hazard of infection is known to increase by a constant, which of course introduces a discontinuity into the PDF that I'm concerned will mess up autodiff in stan if I didn't treat this outcome as a mixture.
>
> If f(x) is the full pdf over the range from [0,a), including both the background exposure and the observed period of elevated exposure from [a-1,a), what I did was to calculate the probability of an infection before A as, where F is the integral of f over the specified range:
>
> Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1) = (F(0 < t < a_i-1)*f(t_1) /F(0 < t < a_i-1)) +  (F(a_i-1 < t < a_i)*f(t_12 /F(a_i-1 < t < a_i)),
>
> which simplifies to just:
>
> Pr(t < a_i | Y = 1) = f(t_1) + f(t_2)
>
> This seems to work but I still somehow don't believe it. So I wanted to check and see if you guys thought this was right.
>
> Sorry for any abuse of notation!
>
> Thanks!
>
> -Jon
>
> On Friday, May 15, 2015 at 10:31:25 AM UTC-4, Jon Zelner wrote:
> > Hi Folks -
> >
> > I'm hoping to implement a weibull survival model for some left-censored current-status data where I have the result of a diagnostic test at age a_i telling me whether an individual was infected before that age, but not when.
> >
> > I'm hoping to model the actual time of infection on the interval from [0,a_i) as a latent variable, using a weibull proportional hazards model. I want to obtain this value to use as input to another model predicting whether an individual develops disease over some time period.
> >
> > The only issue is that there is a single time-varying covariate for a discrete exposure event occurring over a 1-year period that will shift the hazard up by a constant over this period.
> >
> > What I'm worried about is that this discontinuity will mess up stan's gradient calculations for the latent infection time and result in very slow optimization. I'm attaching images showing an example PDF and CDF for an individual with only background exposure up to age 9 and then intensified exposure from age 9-10.
> >
> > One thought I had was to break the calculation into two pieces, treating the latent infection time as a mixture with one component representing the pre-exposure infection times and the other other the post-exposure times. This would result in 2 latent variables, one from [0,A-1) and another from [A-1,A), so that each would have a continuous domain. But I was wondering if there was a simpler approach that might require less in the way of coding gymnastics?
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> > -Jon

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ed,

Thanks for putting the question more clearly than I did, and you're totally right about the notation re: Pr(t | Y = 1). That's correct and the old version is, on reflection, sort of nonsensical.

Just to clarify, the sequence of events you suggest, if we're sticking with the discontinuous hazard, is:

1. Sample t_1 and t_2 from their mutually exclusive distributions with Pr(t) = h(t)s(t) where h and s are the hazard and survival functions for f1 and f2, respectively.

2. Sample g(s | t1,t2) as you describe, i.e. g(s | t1, t2) = F(0, a-1) * g(s | t1) + F(a-1, a) * g(s | t2).

Just wanted to make sure that including the prior weights in the second step isn't somehow tantamount to double-counting the latent infection times. Don't think it is, just want to be sure.

I like your suggestion about a smooth step function too! Seems like that might be less trouble than dealing with the multiple latent vars.

Thanks!

-Jon

>>

>>

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, May 22, 2015 at 1:09:58 AM UTC-4, bee wrote:
> I found there were large differences between sampling results that have different warmup values. Is that OK? I'd like to get the same sampling result with different warmup values.

It's not OK, but it's not unexpected. If you don't warmup enough to render negligible the noise in the adaptation, then you are likely to get different results.

Ben
messages.body_snippet:
On Friday, May 22, 2015 at 1:09:58 AM UTC-4, bee wrote:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan: warmup dependency
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] rstan: warmup dependency
messages.body_plain:
You need to run warmup and sampling long enough to get convergence
and have a high enough effective sample size (n_eff) and an R-hat
near 1 for all parameters.

Usually you need even more than 20 warmup iterations and at least 50 or 100
sampling iterations.  So I'd expect different values with warmups of differing
values below 20n.  And we'd highly recommend running with four chains to
diagnose non-convergence issues.

And thanks for continuing on after finding two bugs right away!

- Bob

Hi,

To gain some experience I have tried different parametrizations in log scale: ka, cl, ke, tlag; ka, v, ke, tlag; ka, cl, v, tlag.  tlag was fixed effect, all other parameters have both fixed and random - see the attached code. On Thu, 21 May 2015 12:06:23 -0400, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi!
>
> There are pros and cons for any of the choices - this is my opinion: From my experience it is always good (numerical wise) to fit ke; or since we are fitting the logs of it, I prefer to fit 1/ke which is the mean residence time; something I understand much better and can hence give better priors. On the contrary, the allometic weight scaling theory stuff is only applicable to Cl and V. Now, what I tend to do, is fit MRTs and then convert them to Cl, apply allometric scaling to Cl and V to finally calculate the patient specific MRT_j. Handling rates or MRTs is a matter of sign-convention on the log-scale...
>
> In principle, I think, you want random effects on all parameters. It usually a compromise of what you can fit with your data and how willing you are to use informative priors on the omegas (variance components of the random effects). Again, this is also a very specific question which can only be answered in the context of your problem and data.
>
> My last point concerning logs: I always calculate the log of the concentrations, so I tend to use the log_diff_exp() / log_sum_exp() functions very often. If you keep all the computations in log space, then all those products become just sums (should be easier for Stan to deal with). The concentration 0 I then always represent as -25, which is reasonably close to 0 on the natural scale.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to implement a hierarchical state space regression model in rstan that follows the methodology of this paper: https://ppw.kuleuven.be/okp/_pdf/Lodewyckx2011AHSSA.pdf

The basic idea is that you have N subjects through time and want to find relationship between y(t,n) and lagged values of y(,n) and  x(t,n) , where t is time,  n is subject id, y is variable of interest, and x are  The regression coefficient beta is assumed to be drawn from a multivariate normal distribution for each individual.

Since its a state space model I tried to code it in terms of "Matt's Trick" found here https://gist.github.com/jrnold/5e0fb240369311bb2f3b to be more efficient.

The code I wrote is does not sample and gets error:
Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is 1.#QNAN:0, but must be finite!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

Any tips or observations on how to fix his error or write better code would be very much appreciated

My code and data are here: https://github.com/samcarlos/Rstan-Hierarchical-State-Space-Dynamics

Thanks in advance,
Sam

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Relation between Categorical and Multinomial Distributions for Order Categorical Regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Relation between Categorical and Multinomial Distributions for Order Categorical Regression
messages.body_plain:
Careful — there’s a subtle difference in the normalizing constant
depending on whether or not you have N realizations of the same
process (binomial or mulitnomial) or N parallel discrete processes
(a product of Bernoulli’s or a product of categoricals).  I don’t think
it will affect sampling for any model we can specify but it’s something
to keep in mind.

For more see the Wikipedia entry,
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Categorical_distribution#Terminology.

On May 23, 2015, at 6:44 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Yes --- you can rewrite categorical or ordered_logistic using
> multinomial.  Same thing with the Bernoulli and binomial.
>
> We should probably have a multinomial version of the ordered
> categorical.  Maybe Rob will put it on his growing list of GLM
> optimizations to take on --- I know they're redoing the ordered
> logistic itself to make it faster.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On May 23, 2015, at 1:42 PM, Cody Ross <ctr...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:
>>
>> In Stan we can write an ordered logistic model with a single ecological-level predictor:
>> for (n in 1:N){
>> Outcome[n] ~ ordered_logistic( (Beta[1] + Beta[2]*X[Cluster[n]]), C);
>> }
>>
>> Which is short for the more explicit model:
>> for (n in 1:N) {
>> real eta;
>> eta <- Beta[1] + Beta[2]*X[Cluster[n]];
>> scrap[1] <- 1 - inv_logit(eta - C[1]);
>> for (k in 2:(K-1))
>> scrap[k] <- inv_logit(eta - C[k-1]) - inv_logit(eta - C[k]);
>> scrap[K] <- inv_logit(eta - C[K-1]);
>> Outcome[n] ~ categorical(scrap);
>> }
>>
>> Now, the question is... since the predictor is at the ecological level, could we re-write the model for efficiency by rewriting the individual-level data at the cluster level... so instead of the data looking like:
>> Outcome[1] = 3
>> Outcome[2] = 5
>> etc...
>>
>> We have cluster-level counts as vectors, defined simply by summing the number of outcomes of each category in the given cluster:
>> OutcomeCluster[1] = (10, 3, 50, 30, 2)'
>> OutcomeCluster[2] = (12, 45, 40, 35, 4)'
>>
>> And then change the model to:
>> for (l in 1:L) {
>> real eta;
>> eta <- Beta[1] + Beta[2]*X[l];
>> scrap[1] <- 1 - inv_logit(eta - C[1]);
>> for (k in 2:(K-1))
>> scrap[k] <- inv_logit(eta - C[k-1]) - inv_logit(eta - C[k]);
>> scrap[K] <- inv_logit(eta - C[K-1]);
>> OutcomeCluster[l] ~ multinomial(scrap);
>> }
>>
>> In other words... instead of updating the LP accumulator N times with the categorical distribution, can we update it only L times with the multinomial, since the categorical distribution is just a special case of the multinomial with count equals 1?
>>
>> --

>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical State Space Dynamics
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical State Space Dynamics
messages.body_plain:
When I tried running your example I got a different error message:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is nan:0, but must be finite!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
 Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.

I've been trying to strip down your model to figure out what's causing this, but no luck so far. There's definitely a couple places you could probably clean things up, e.g. inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001) is probably way too wide, I don't think you need to create y_data_observed, but can instead do something like:

for (n in 1:N) {
    for (t in (2+L):T){
        if(!y_data_indicator_missing[t,n])
            y_data[t,n]~normal(theta[n,t] , sigma_y);
    }
}

(once you get everything working you can add back in your unobserved data the same way, or perhaps more robustly, sample it in post-processing step in R or in the generated quantities block in Stan.)

You also shouldn't need to transform sigmasq_y to sigma_y; you can just put a prior on sigma_y (see manual for examples). Does sigmasq_beta get used?

Overall, I'd suggest making your model as simple as possible, fixing all the parameters at reasonable values (you can do this by moving them to the data block and then passing in fixed values -- it's no problem to leave the sample statement in the model block, it won't do anything!) and trying to get something that at least samples, then add features of the model back in one by one until you figure out what's causing the issue.

Happy to try to figure out what's wrong with a simpler model, just send it back to the list. But do please try to indent your code for readability. ;)

messages.body_plain:
Yes, the problem is primarily related to the compilation of Stan.

Boost 1.58 broke backward compatibility in their lazy evaluation
library Fusion, which is used heavily in the Spirit Qi parser.

I've modified our parser code to match 1.58, with the consequence
that it no longer works with Boost versions before 1.56 (previous Stan was
at 1.55 to match BH before it changed).  It's passing tests on the Mac,
but not on Windows.  Here's the pull request, which references the branch:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/1460

It's a holiday weekend here in NY, but we'll get this sorted out on the Stan
C++ side later this week.  A patch or updated version of RStan should follow.

Sorry the R library compatibility has been a problem.  We weren't
anticipating an update of BH, which skipped 1.56 and 1.57 updates,
but we should've been ready with compatible code for existing Boost
releases.

- Bob

I cleaned up code without y_data_observed (I'll include it later but since data is complete, I'll ignore it) here: https://github.com/samcarlos/Rstan-Hierarchical-State-Space-Dynamics/blob/master/HSSD_Test_1.R.  The code gets the error:

Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is 1.#QNAN:0, but must be finite!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.

Not sure why we're getting different errors.

I then tried to make more simple by modeling theta as a unit root process (no lagged values of theta other than (t-1) ) and this sampled fine. Because of this it seems like including lagged values of theta is causing a hiccup in sampling.  The code for this is here: https://github.com/samcarlos/Rstan-Hierarchical-State-Space-Dynamics/blob/master/HSSD_Test_1_noLaggedTheta.R .

When you say "fix all values at reasonable values", do you mean explicitly declaring something like : "sigmasq_y <- 1" as opposed to  "sigmasq_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001)"?

Thanks Again!,
Sam

On Sun, May 24, 2015 at 6:20 PM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:

> When I tried running your example I got a different error message:
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is nan:0, but must be finite!
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
> Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
>
>
> Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
>  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
>
>
> I've been trying to strip down your model to figure out what's causing this, but no luck so far. There's definitely a couple places you could probably clean things up, e.g. inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001) is probably way too wide, I don't think you need to create y_data_observed, but can instead do something like:
>
> for (n in 1:N) {
>     for (t in (2+L):T){
>         if(!y_data_indicator_missing[t,n])
>             y_data[t,n]~normal(theta[n,t] , sigma_y);
>     }
> }
>
> (once you get everything working you can add back in your unobserved data the same way, or perhaps more robustly, sample it in post-processing step in R or in the generated quantities block in Stan.)
>
> You also shouldn't need to transform sigmasq_y to sigma_y; you can just put a prior on sigma_y (see manual for examples). Does sigmasq_beta get used?
>
> Overall, I'd suggest making your model as simple as possible, fixing all the parameters at reasonable values (you can do this by moving them to the data block and then passing in fixed values -- it's no problem to leave the sample statement in the model block, it won't do anything!) and trying to get something that at least samples, then add features of the model back in one by one until you figure out what's causing the issue.
>
> Happy to try to figure out what's wrong with a simpler model, just send it back to the list. But do please try to indent your code for readability. ;)
>
> On Sat, May 23, 2015 at 10:17 AM, Sam Weiss <samc...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hello,
> >
> > I'm trying to implement a hierarchical state space regression model in rstan that follows the methodology of this paper: https://ppw.kuleuven.be/okp/_pdf/Lodewyckx2011AHSSA.pdf

> > Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is 1.#QNAN:0, but must be finite!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
> >
> >
> > Any tips or observations on how to fix his error or write better code would be very much appreciated
> >
> > My code and data are here: https://github.com/samcarlos/Rstan-Hierarchical-State-Space-Dynamics
> >
> > Thanks in advance,

messages.subject: How to Define Regularizing Laplace Priors in Multi-level Models?
messages.subject_clean: How to Define Regularizing Laplace Priors in Multi-level Models?
messages.body_plain:
Say one would like to model something using a basic model:
Y[n]~ Dist(Link(theta[n]))

theta[n] <- alpha + X[n]*beta
where alpha is an intercept, X a row vector of predictors, and beta a vector of parameters.

But if X is long and we only expect a small number of effects, we can use regularizing priors:
beta ~ DoubleExponential(0, 0.5)

But... if we have multi-level structure things start to look weird to me:
Y[n]~ Dist(Link(theta[n]))

theta[n] <- alpha + X[n]*beta[cluster[n]]

beta[c] <- MuBeta + DeltaBeta[c];

MuBeta ~ DoubleExponential(0, 0.5)

DeltaBeta[c] ~ Normal(zeros, SigmaDeltaBeta)

SigmaDeltaBeta ~ HalfCauchy(0,1)

Which seems not quite right to me...

I think I'd like to be able to do something like:
(MuBeta + DeltaBeta[c]) ~ DoubleExponential(0, 0.5)

instead of defining the double exp prior only over MuBeta...

1) Can I do this in Stan?
2a) Do I need to do some Jacobian adjustment if I do?
2b) If so, how do I figure out what the adjustment should be?
3) Most importantly, is there a better way to implement the kind of model I am suggesting here?

Thanks ahead of time!

> When you say "fix all values at reasonable values", do you mean explicitly declaring something like : "sigmasq_y <- 1" as opposed to  "sigmasq_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001)"?

You can't assign to a parameter in the model block but you could do this:
transformed data {
  real sigmasq_y;
  sigmasq_y <- 1;
}

But I think it's easier to play around with values by putting it in as data;
data {
  real sigmasq_y;
}

Because then you can leave the sampling statement in the model block (that's what I was saying about it not affecting anything) and mess around with different values passed in as stan.dat. (You'll need to remove the declaration from the parameters block.)

Maybe your issue is theta_innovation? You declare it as:
matrix[T,N] theta_innovation;

But then what does this do? Isn't the indexing off?
for(n in 1:N) theta_innovation[n]~normal(0,1);

Maybe this is what you meant?
for(t in 1:T) for(n in 1:N) theta_innovation[t,n]~normal(0,1);

Or this?
for(t in 1:T)
theta_innovation[t]~normal(0,1);

It seems to sample now! 300 iterations took 125 seconds.

Best,
Seth

messages.body_plain: In addition to what you listed, lp__ also includes Jacobian adjustments for bounded parameters (which are sampled on the unconstrained scale, remember). So whatever you calculate "manually" will be different from lp__ (even if you take account of the constants that are dropped), unless there are no constrained parameters in your model (which is not the case for you, as the "sigma"-parameters are constrained to be positive).

messages.body_plain:
Answers inline

On Monday, May 25, 2015 at 5:24:04 PM UTC+3, James Camac wrote:
> Hi all,
> I've been searching through this forum and through the manual in how I can set up cross validation in stan.
> But unfortunately I haven't been able to find much besides approximations using WAIC etc.

How about this (which despite it's filename, is about cross-validation, too)?
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf

> The approach I've taken is first to break up the data into 10 folds. I then hold 1 fold out and use the 9/10ths to fit the data.
> Below outlines how I'm attempting to do cross validation for a single fit/held out combination, with the plan to repeat this 10 times, each with a different fold held out (i.e. so all folds are held out once).

10-fold-CV is fine and your code looks like same as in the above mentioned paper, except that you sum the terms (see below). You could probably also use leave-one-out cross-validation as described in
in the above mentioned paper.

> If what I have done is correct, stan should calculate the summed log likelihood of both the fitted data (log_lik_fit_total) and the heldout data (log_li_tilde_total).

I would usually recommend not to sum log_lik's, but return log_lik for each test observation and combine test observation log_liks outside of Stan, and use values to look at outliers and compute, e.g., variance of the CV estimate. But maybe you want to use sums to save memory?

> Which when ran across all heldout combinations gives me 10 log likelihoods. I can then use some summary statistic (e.g. mean or median) or even plot the distribution of these log likelihoods as a way of comparing the fit or predictive fit relative to other cross validated models (e.g. the same model, same priors, but with a different measure of growth_dt), or in the case of nested models where a predictor (e.g. a2,b2,c2) is left out, using a log ratio approach.

Yes. You can also compute standard errors as described in the above mentioned paper.

> Side notes (potentially stupid questions):
> My understanding is that stan's lp__ is the sum of the log likelihood of the model + log probability of the priors - constants. i.e. The log posterior - constants.
> How could this, or the standard log posterior be calculated in the generated quantities as a way of checking my calculations of the log likelihoods are correct? Or is this just a stupid nonsensical thing to do?

This was answered by Luc.

> Also, I've seen it mentioned many times that lp__ should not be used in model comparison. But what if the model is structurally the same, with the same priors and the only difference is one of the predictors (e.g. growth_dt in my model) is changed with a different way of calculating growth_dt? If the prior probability remains the same, can't lp__ be used to compare models by looking at absolute differences?

Even then it would not be a good estimate for the future predictive performance.

Aki

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical model & cross validation in stan
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical model & cross validation in stan
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Luc and Aki,
That makes a lot of sense re: lp__ and why I couldn't replicate it in the generated quantities.

Aki, I actually saw your paper and used it as a basis for how I constructed my model. The only reason I'm not monitoring the log lik for each observation is that it chews through a lot of RAM and makes the output file 4 times as big. Which isn't a problem if its just a single model I'm running. But I need to run 40 model variants, each with the 10 kfold cross validation.
Also because the models take quiet some time to run... I'm not sure actually doing LOO would be efficient here (i'm working with close to 200,000 observations).

I'm now playing around with altering the stepsize and adapt_delta to see if I can get any extra computational efficiency - more out of interest then neccessity.

My question is whether I can simply run the model for 50 iterations (i.e. not converged) to test how altering stepsize (i.e. 0.01, 0.0001) and/or adapt_delta (i.e. 0.9, 0.99) influences the speed of the warm up and the tree depth and n_divergence. It seems that when I reduce the stepsize i'm getting more n_divergence. The other weird thing that happens when I alter these settings is that as soon as the model finishes adapting and starts sampling the tree depth jumps up the the maximum... Is this simply because I haven't allowed enough iterations in warm up?

In other words... to really see the effect of these settings should I be running the model for what I usually do with this model - 2000 iterations where it generally stabilizes by ~1000 mark.

Hey Seth,

I coded the lagged_thetas in a different way here :https://github.com/samcarlos/Rstan-Hierarchical-State-Space-Dynamics/blob/master/HSSD_Test_1.R . It compiles now!  But It does get stuck every other chain (where it only samples the same values for each iteration).

However, computing a covariance matrix with num_vars*num_lags+num_lags-1 seems to be a computational burden if including dozens of variables with lots of lags.. What do you think the effect of not including a covariance matrix Sigma_beta and just have it be a variance of all coefficients.

instead of :
 for(n in 1:N) beta[n]~multi_normal(mu_beta,Sigma_beta);

It will be this:
 for(n in 1:N) for(p in 1:num_vars) beta[n,p]~normal(mu_beta[p],Sigma_beta_vetcor[p]);

The posterior distribution will still have correlated beta distribution, but it won't be explicit in the prior.

Thanks again,
Sam

messages.body_plain:
> On May 26, 2015, at 8:12 AM, James Camac <james...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Luc and Aki,
> That makes a lot of sense re: lp__ and why I couldn't replicate it in the generated quantities.
>
> Aki, I actually saw your paper and used it as a basis for how I constructed my model. The only reason I'm not monitoring the log lik for each observation is that it chews through a lot of RAM and makes the output file 4 times as big. Which isn't a problem if its just a single model I'm running. But I need to run 40 model variants, each with the 10 kfold cross validation.
> Also because the models take quiet some time to run... I'm not sure actually doing LOO would be efficient here (i'm working with close to 200,000 observations).
>
> I'm now playing around with altering the stepsize and adapt_delta to see if I can get any extra computational efficiency - more out of interest then neccessity.

What you want to do is test that you get the same result with smaller
stepsizes.  That'll make sure the step size isn't bounding you out of tails
you care about in meaningful ways.

> My question is whether I can simply run the model for 50 iterations (i.e. not converged) to test how altering stepsize (i.e. 0.01, 0.0001) and/or adapt_delta (i.e. 0.9, 0.99) influences the speed of the warm up and the tree depth and n_divergence. It seems that when I reduce the stepsize i'm getting more n_divergence. The other weird thing that happens when I alter these settings is that as soon as the model finishes adapting and starts sampling the tree depth jumps up the the maximum... Is this simply because I haven't allowed enough iterations in warm up?

There's a final step size warmup with the final mass matrix, so that's
probably getting shrunk.  If you ran warmup longer, you'd see the same
increase in tree depth.

If the model runs into max tree depth, you either want to reparameterize
or up the tree depth so you don't devolve to a random walk.

> In other words... to really see the effect of these settings should I be running the model for what I usually do with this model - 2000 iterations where it generally stabilizes by ~1000 mark.

Yes.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On May 25, 2015, at 2:32 PM, Cody Ross <ctr...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:
>
> Say one would like to model something using a basic model:
> Y[n]~ Dist(Link(theta[n]))
>
> theta[n] <- alpha + X[n]*beta
> where alpha is an intercept, X a row vector of predictors, and beta a vector of parameters.
>
> But if X is long and we only expect a small number of effects, we can use regularizing priors:
> beta ~ DoubleExponential(0, 0.5)

Just to be clear here --- Stan's not going to drive parameter
estimates to zero, but it may be close in either optimization or
sampling.

> But... if we have multi-level structure things start to look weird to me:
> Y[n]~ Dist(Link(theta[n]))
>
> theta[n] <- alpha + X[n]*beta[cluster[n]]
>
> beta[c] <- MuBeta + DeltaBeta[c];
>
> MuBeta ~ DoubleExponential(0, 0.5)
>
> DeltaBeta[c] ~ Normal(zeros, SigmaDeltaBeta)
>
> SigmaDeltaBeta ~ HalfCauchy(0,1)
>
> Which seems not quite right to me...

Looks OK to me.

The more usual way to write all this would be:

  beta ~ normal(mu_beta, sigma_beta);

  mu_beta ~ double_exponential(0, 0.5);

But it's more efficient in the non-centered parameterization:

  beta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

  beta <- mu_beta + sigma_beta * beta_raw;

> I think I'd like to be able to do something like:
> (MuBeta + DeltaBeta[c]) ~ DoubleExponential(0, 0.5)

This looks wrong --- if you put that in a loop, you'll be
giving a prior to MuBeta multiple times.

> instead of defining the double exp prior only over MuBeta...
>
> 1) Can I do this in Stan?
> 2a) Do I need to do some Jacobian adjustment if I do?
> 2b) If so, how do I figure out what the adjustment should be?
> 3) Most importantly, is there a better way to implement the kind of model I am suggesting here?
>

Maybe just an easier way to think about it --- see above.

- Bob

messages.subject: Jolly-Seber model, state-space representation
messages.subject_clean: Jolly-Seber model, state-space representation
messages.body_plain:
Hi list,

I'm trying to code the state-space representation of the JS model for capture-mark-recapture data in stan and I think I've reached the (current) limit of my mathematical ability with regards to marginalization of the (latent) discrete parameter.

The basic model is represented by three Bernoulli sampling statements.

i corresponds to observed individual, t is the point in time, p is sampling/observation probability, y_{i,t} is the observed state (0 or 1), z is the latent discrete state (0 or 1), phi is the probability of survival from t to t+1, and gamma is the probability of being "born" (recruitment).  There are no "zombies" (individuals can't be reborn).

y_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(p_{t} * z_{i,t})
z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(z_{i,t-1} * phi_{t-1} + (1 - z{i,t-1}) * gamma_{t})
z_{i,1} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{1}).

Note that I can also write z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{t} + (phi_{t} - gamma{t}) * z_{i,t}) instead of the second sampling statement following Royle and Dorazio's "Hierarchical modeling and inference in ecology" book. I've also attached a relevant 2012 paper from King titled "A review of Bayesian state-space modelling of capture–recapture–recovery data". The most relevant section is 2.2 (Estimating abundance).

Given that I want to implement this in stan, I need to marginalize out the discrete parameter z. This is where me problem comes in: I don't know how to do this.

I've read over the CJS model implemented in the stan manual (page 111), and it has been quite helpful for better understanding what I'd probably have to do. I'm just stuck on how to modify that to end with the JS model via the introduction of recruitment.

Any advice would be highly appreciated.

Cheers,

Peter Smits

messages.subject: Re: Jolly-Seber model, state-space representation
messages.subject_clean: Jolly-Seber model, state-space representation
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, May 26, 2015 at 4:54:36 PM UTC-4, Peter Smits wrote:
> Hi list,
>
> I'm trying to code the state-space representation of the JS model for capture-mark-recapture data in stan and I think I've reached the (current) limit of my mathematical ability with regards to marginalization of the (latent) discrete parameter.
>
> The basic model is represented by three Bernoulli sampling statements.
>
> i corresponds to observed individual, t is the point in time, p is sampling/observation probability, y_{i,t} is the observed state (0 or 1), z is the latent discrete state (0 or 1), phi is the probability of survival from t to t+1, and gamma is the probability of being "born" (recruitment).  There are no "zombies" (individuals can't be reborn).
>
> y_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(p_{t} * z_{i,t})
> z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(z_{i,t-1} * phi_{t-1} + (1 - z{i,t-1}) * gamma_{t})
> z_{i,1} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{1}).
>
> Note that I can also write z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{t} + (phi_{t} - gamma{t}) * z_{i,t}) instead of the second sampling statement following Royle and Dorazio's "Hierarchical modeling and inference in ecology" book. I've also attached a relevant 2012 paper from King titled "A review of Bayesian state-space modelling of capture–recapture–recovery data". The most relevant section is 2.2 (Estimating abundance).
>
> Given that I want to implement this in stan, I need to marginalize out the discrete parameter z. This is where me problem comes in: I don't know how to do this.
>
>
> I've read over the CJS model implemented in the stan manual (page 111), and it has been quite helpful for better understanding what I'd probably have to do. I'm just stuck on how to modify that to end with the JS model via the introduction of recruitment.

The summation over 'z' in CJS runs over all possible unobserved outcomes after the final observation.  Similarly the summation in JS would need to run over all possible unobserved outcomes from the first possible birth up until tagging... so for one individual unobserved at t=1,2,3 and observed at t=4:

gamma(t_1) * phi(t_1) * phi(t_2) * phi(t_3) + gamma(t_2) * phi(t_2) * phi(t_3) + gamma(t_3) * phi(t_3) + gamma(t_4)

if the individual is available for recapture after birth, this becomes

gamma(t_1) * (1-p(t_1))*phi(t_1) * (1-p(t_2))* phi(t_2) * (1-p(t_3))*phi(t_3) + gamma(t_2) * (1-p(t_2))*phi(t_2) * (1-p(t_3))*phi(t_3) + gamma(t_3) * (1-p(t_3))*phi(t_3) + gamma(t_4)

That's "born at time 1 and survived 1 to 2, 2 to 3, and 3 to 4" plus "born at time 2 and survived 2 to 3 and 3 to 4" plus... etc... In both cases parts of the calculation repeat, so you can do a running calculation of the "survive and not capture" running backwards in time, keep it on the log scale, and just add the gamma component to each one, something like:

for ( t in 3:1) {
   A <- log( phi(t) ) + log(1-p(t)) + A
  B[t] <- A[t] +  log(gamma(t))
}
increment_log_prob(sum(B) + gamma(t))

It's late and I didn't check any of that but that's the gist of it.

Krzysztof

>
> Any advice would be highly appreciated.
>
> Cheers,
>
> Peter Smits

messages.body_plain:
Wait, are you asking about the parameter lambda or the data n?

The rate parameter of the Poisson distribution lambda can be real
(from the manual p. 356):

real poisson_log(ints n, reals lambda)
    The log Poisson probability mass of n given rate lambda

It's the observations that are giving you trouble because they need to
be integer:
    real <lower=0> I[nobs];

But that doesn't seem like it'll be a problem for your model, will it?
I don't have your data to try, but I think this should work:
    int<lower=0> I[nobs];

Best,
Seth

Krzysztof,

I went back and read over Royle and Dorazio's book, and given what you've written and what I've pried out of that here is where I am at. I'm using a time forward form of the model and I've created "k" which is the related to recruitability. I've also, for the sake of simplicity, assumed time constant probabilities.

z_{i, t} = phi * z_{i, t - 1} + gamma * k

where k = prod_{k = 1}^{t - 1} (1 - z_{i, k}).

Then I've just done y_{i, t} ~ Bern(p * z_{i, t}), where p is still preservation probability.

Assuming I've done this right, I run the simulated data set through the model. What comes out the other side, however, is super unconstrained. Generally, the true values fall in the credible interval. So I think this is right? Thoughts?

Attached at a stan file, an R simulation script, and the bash script I use to run the model. Beyond the vagaries of directory trees, these should work.

My data set is a set of global fossil occurrences from the Paleozoic <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleozoic>. Each time point is a geologic stage and each individual is a brachiopod genus. The data set is available for free via the Paleobiology Database <http://fossilworks.org/?page=paleodb>. Systems like brachiopods are great because they have higher preservation rate/potential than most other groups of shelly marine invertebrates. It is a non-standard data set for ecology, but fairly normal for paleobiology.

Cheers,

Peter

messages.subject_clean: different constraints for vector elements
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Is there a way to place different constraints for the individual elements of a vector when declaring that vector?

That is, we can ensure positive values of both elements of a 2-D vector by declaring:

vector<lower=0>[2] muTb;

But I would like to declare a 2D vector where only the first element has a 0 lower bound - is this possible?

I need to declare such a vector (and not two scalars) because it is used as the (mean vector) argument in the sampling of a multi_normal distribution.  The first variable needs to be positive as it is used as an argument to log() in the transformed parameters block, but the second variable can be negative or positive.

Thanks,
-Rahul

model {

  muTb[1] <- positive_thing;

  ...

Or you could probably reparameterize in terms of the logarithm of the positive parameter, and in the model block take the antilog of that as needed.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Jolly-Seber model, state-space representation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Jolly-Seber model, state-space representation
messages.body_plain:
I don't think the final model captured what you wanted
because it's not in the form of a marginalization.

More below.

> On May 26, 2015, at 4:54 PM, Peter Smits <thesti...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi list,
>
> I'm trying to code the state-space representation of the JS model for capture-mark-recapture data in stan and I think I've reached the (current) limit of my mathematical ability with regards to marginalization of the (latent) discrete parameter.
>
> The basic model is represented by three Bernoulli sampling statements.
>
> i corresponds to observed individual, t is the point in time, p is sampling/observation probability, y_{i,t} is the observed state (0 or 1), z is the latent discrete state (0 or 1), phi is the probability of survival from t to t+1, and gamma is the probability of being "born" (recruitment).  There are no "zombies" (individuals can't be reborn).
>
> y_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(p_{t} * z_{i,t})
> z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(z_{i,t-1} * phi_{t-1} + (1 - z{i,t-1}) * gamma_{t})
> z_{i,1} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{1}).

Here's the way to think about this:

  p(y, z, phi, p, gamma)

  = p(phi, p, gamma)   // prior

    * PROD_{i in 1:N} bern(z[i,1] | gamma[1])

                      * PROD_{t in 2:T} bern(z[i,t] | z[i,t-1] * phi[t-1] + (1 - z[i, t-1]) * gamma[t])

                                        * bern(y[i,t] | p[t] * z[i,t])

Then the goal is to marginalize out the the parameter z[i,t] representing if
individual i is alive at time t to get:

  p(y, phi, p, gamma)

It's both tricky and tractable because of the constraints, which I would
think should ensure that z[i,] must be a sequence of contiguous 1s that
includes all t such that y[i,t] = 1.

   * if y[i,t] = 1 then z[i,t] = 1

   * if z[i,t] = 0 and any z[i,t-1] = 1, then z[i, t + n ] = 0 for all n > 0

In words, z[i,] has to be a sequence of contiguous 1s that includes
all t such that y[i,t] = 1.

So what you need to do is add all the probability for the legal z configurations
together (of which there are luckily at most T^2 due to constraints).

This is quite a bit trickier to code than the one in the manual, but has the
same principle.  You want to define a function

  // compute log likelihood of y for a single individual
  real state_space_log(int[] y, vector phi, vector p, vector gamma) {
    i.e., big sum (using log-sum-exp) over legal z values
    vector[first_sighting[i] * (T - last_sighting[i])] lp;
    int i;
    i <- 0;
    for (t_first_alive in 1:first_siting[i]) {
      for (t_last_alive in (last_siting[i] + 1):T) {
        log_prob[i] <- log prob for config, which involves more looping,
                       but now z[i,t] == (t >= t_first_alive && t <= t_last_alive)
        i <- i + 1;
    return log_sum_exp(log_prob);
  }

It'll probably help to create an auxliary data structure of first and last
sightings, because you know it has to be all 1s before that, so then there's
just the choice of when the individual was born (which can be before the
first time point --- that's gamma[1], right?) and when the individual died (which
can be after the last time point).

And then the model is super simple.

  for (i in 1:I)
    y[i] ~ state_space(phi, p, gamma);

Sorry it's such a hassle!  If there's only 30 time periods and 1000 individuals, it
should be tractable enough to sample.

If this isn't enough of a hint, I can help out more.  I'm going to send
a different message with my implementation of the Dorazio-Royle species-site
occupancy model, which involves another marginalization.  I really want
to see all these ecology models working.

- Bob

> Note that I can also write z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{t} + (phi_{t} - gamma{t}) * z_{i,t}) instead of the second sampling statement following Royle and Dorazio's "Hierarchical modeling and inference in ecology" book. I've also attached a relevant 2012 paper from King titled "A review of Bayesian state-space modelling of capture–recapture–recovery data". The most relevant section is 2.2 (Estimating abundance).
>
> Given that I want to implement this in stan, I need to marginalize out the discrete parameter z. This is where me problem comes in: I don't know how to do this.
>
> I've read over the CJS model implemented in the stan manual (page 111), and it has been quite helpful for better understanding what I'd probably have to do. I'm just stuck on how to modify that to end with the JS model via the introduction of recruitment.
>
> Any advice would be highly appreciated.
>
> Cheers,
>
> Peter Smits
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for the comments. After contemplating the model last night, you're total right in saying the previous model isn't capturing what I thought it was capturing.

Let me see if I'm understanding you're suggestion for how to implement this. I've included the first_capture and last_capture functions from the manual in order to get that information. The key is then estimating the probability of z being 1 during times NOT captured in the minimum observed duration, correct?

Through example: this observed capture history, 0000111001111000, corresponds to the minimum observed duration of 0000111111111000. Thus, the probabilities z = 1 of the 4 leading and trailing time points need to be calculated, correct?

This would lead to something similar the prob_uncaptured in the manual example of the CJS model but now with the gamma term.

Let's see if I get this right:
For observations before to the first observation
for y[i, t=1] = 0: Pr(z[i, t] = 1) = k[t=1] = gamma[t=1] * p[t=1]
for y[i, t > 1] = 0: Pr(z[i, t > 1]) = k[t] = gamma[t] * p[t] + p[t] * (1 - phi[t - 1]) * k[t - 1]

Given that things can't be re-born/become zombies, for observations after the first observation it is possible to just use the prob_uncaptured function from the manual, right? I'm suspicious I've forgotten something key...

Honestly, I'd appreciate all the help I can get. This list and its archives have been super helpful in making Stan super accessible. I've been able to implement a lot of models, but this is the first time I've had to deal with marginalization (I don't come from a math/stats background).

Cheers,

Peter

On Thursday, May 28, 2015 at 12:56:20 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't think the final model captured what you wanted
> because it's not in the form of a marginalization.
>
> More below.
>
> > On May 26, 2015, at 4:54 PM, Peter Smits <thesti...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi list,
> >
> > I'm trying to code the state-space representation of the JS model for capture-mark-recapture data in stan and I think I've reached the (current) limit of my mathematical ability with regards to marginalization of the (latent) discrete parameter.
> >
> > The basic model is represented by three Bernoulli sampling statements.
> >
> > i corresponds to observed individual, t is the point in time, p is sampling/observation probability, y_{i,t} is the observed state (0 or 1), z is the latent discrete state (0 or 1), phi is the probability of survival from t to t+1, and gamma is the probability of being "born" (recruitment).  There are no "zombies" (individuals can't be reborn).
> >
> > y_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(p_{t} * z_{i,t})
> > z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(z_{i,t-1} * phi_{t-1} + (1 - z{i,t-1}) * gamma_{t})
> > z_{i,1} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{1}).
>
> Here's the way to think about this:
>
>   p(y, z, phi, p, gamma)
>
>   = p(phi, p, gamma)   // prior
>
>     * PROD_{i in 1:N} bern(z[i,1] | gamma[1])
>
>                       * PROD_{t in 2:T} bern(z[i,t] | z[i,t-1] * phi[t-1] + (1 - z[i, t-1]) * gamma[t])
>
>                                         * bern(y[i,t] | p[t] * z[i,t])
>
> Then the goal is to marginalize out the the parameter z[i,t] representing if
> individual i is alive at time t to get:
>
>   p(y, phi, p, gamma)
>
> It's both tricky and tractable because of the constraints, which I would
> think should ensure that z[i,] must be a sequence of contiguous 1s that
> includes all t such that y[i,t] = 1.
>
>    * if y[i,t] = 1 then z[i,t] = 1
>
>    * if z[i,t] = 0 and any z[i,t-1] = 1, then z[i, t + n ] = 0 for all n > 0
>
> In words, z[i,] has to be a sequence of contiguous 1s that includes
> all t such that y[i,t] = 1.
>
> So what you need to do is add all the probability for the legal z configurations
> together (of which there are luckily at most T^2 due to constraints).
>
> This is quite a bit trickier to code than the one in the manual, but has the
> same principle.  You want to define a function
>
>   // compute log likelihood of y for a single individual
>   real state_space_log(int[] y, vector phi, vector p, vector gamma) {
>     i.e., big sum (using log-sum-exp) over legal z values
>     vector[first_sighting[i] * (T - last_sighting[i])] lp;
>     int i;
>     i <- 0;
>     for (t_first_alive in 1:first_siting[i]) {
>       for (t_last_alive in (last_siting[i] + 1):T) {
>         log_prob[i] <- log prob for config, which involves more looping,
>                        but now z[i,t] == (t >= t_first_alive && t <= t_last_alive)
>         i <- i + 1;
>     return log_sum_exp(log_prob);
>   }
>
> It'll probably help to create an auxliary data structure of first and last
> sightings, because you know it has to be all 1s before that, so then there's
> just the choice of when the individual was born (which can be before the
> first time point --- that's gamma[1], right?) and when the individual died (which
> can be after the last time point).
>
> And then the model is super simple.
>
>   for (i in 1:I)
>     y[i] ~ state_space(phi, p, gamma);
>
> Sorry it's such a hassle!  If there's only 30 time periods and 1000 individuals, it
> should be tractable enough to sample.
>
> If this isn't enough of a hint, I can help out more.  I'm going to send
> a different message with my implementation of the Dorazio-Royle species-site
> occupancy model, which involves another marginalization.  I really want
> to see all these ecology models working.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > Note that I can also write z_{i,t} ~ Bernoulli(gamma_{t} + (phi_{t} - gamma{t}) * z_{i,t}) instead of the second sampling statement following Royle and Dorazio's "Hierarchical modeling and inference in ecology" book. I've also attached a relevant 2012 paper from King titled "A review of Bayesian state-space modelling of capture–recapture–recovery data". The most relevant section is 2.2 (Estimating abundance).
> >
> > Given that I want to implement this in stan, I need to marginalize out the discrete parameter z. This is where me problem comes in: I don't know how to do this.
> >
> > I've read over the CJS model implemented in the stan manual (page 111), and it has been quite helpful for better understanding what I'd probably have to do. I'm just stuck on how to modify that to end with the JS model via the introduction of recruitment.
> >
> > Any advice would be highly appreciated.
> >
> > Cheers,
> >
> > Peter Smits

messages.body_plain:
The key is this simple relation:

  p(a) = SUM_b p(a,b)

To make a simpler case, let's say you have 5 observation times
and have observed the animal at time=2 and time=3, that is,

observed captures y: 01100

Then you get the following options for z

   01100  first_alive=2  last_alive=3
   01110
   01111
   11100
   11110
   11111  first_alive=1  last_alive=5

And what you need to do is compute p(y,z) for each of these z
on the log scale in an array,

  lp[1] = log p(y=01100, z=01100 | p, phi, gamma)
  lp[2] = log p(y=01100, z=01110 | p, phi, gamma)
  ...
  lp[6] = log p(y=01100, z=11111 | p, phi, gamma)

then use:

  increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));

because

  log_sum_exp(lp) = log (exp(lp[1]) + exp(lp[2]) + ... + exp(lp[6]))

                  = log (p[1] + ... p[6])

where p[1] = exp(lp[1]) is the probability of y and the first config of z.

So you take the sum of the probabilities of each pair of y and legal z
and add them up then take the log.  It's just log_sum_exp does it more
efficiently and has more arithmetic stability and accuracy.

The trick is that you're going to need to do this in a double loop over
first_alive and last_alive.

I'm busy right now trying to get the latest RStan patched for Windows,
but when that's done, I'll implement the model and do some data
simulation for this.  It's not that difficult algebraically, but it's a lot of fiddly
coding with indexes.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

I think I'm starting to get this. Would the state_space(...) function then look like (attached also in a stan file)? I apologize for poor code.

  real state_space_log(int[] y, vector phi, vector p, vector gamma) {

    vector[first_capture(y) * (size(y) - last_capture(y))] lp;
    int i;
    i <- 1;

    for(t_first_alive in 1:first_capture(y)) {
      for (t_last_alive in (last_capture(y) + 1):size(y)) {
        vector[2 * size(y)] sl;
        int z[size(y)];

        for(l in 1:size(y)) {
          z[l] <- 0;
        }
        for(a in t_first_alive:t_last_alive)
          z[a] <- 1;

        sl[1] <- bernoulli_log(z[1], gamma[1]);
        for(j in 2:size(y)) {
          sl[j] <- bernoulli_log(z[j], z[j - 1] * (1 - phi[j - 1]) +
                                       gamma[j] * (1 - z[j - 1]));
        }
        for(k in (size(y) + 1):(2 * size(y))) {
          sl[k] <- bernoulli_log(y[k], z[k] * p[k]);
        }

        lp[i] <- log_sum_exp(sl);

        i <- i + 1;
      }
    }

    return log_sum_exp(lp);
  }

Cheers,

Peter

I think that's getting closer, but I still don't think it's
quite right.  The z and y should be added together in the
same component and there should only be one log_sum_exp, where
the elements are the log likelihoods for each possible configuration
of hidden state of aliveness that is consistent with captures.

You also want to assign and save first_capture and last_capture
rather than recomputing.

I'll try to work out the full example tomorrow.

I took a look at that Ruth King paper and it's great.  I love
it when domain scientists write clearly enough from a basic enough
level on the science side that I can understand what's going on.
She talks about the marginalization required to generate the likelihood
function, which is what you'd typically need for optimization (for [penalized]
MLE estimation).

- Bob
