messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Theoretic question about HMC
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Theoretic question about HMC
messages.body_plain:
Let’s review the basics of HMC.  We have our target distribution, pi(q) = exp(-V(q)),
and the conditional distribution of the momenta, pi(p|q) = exp(-T(q, p)).  The HMC
transition is then (i) sample the momenta, p ~ pi(p|q) (ii) evolve using Hamiltonian flow,
(q, p) -> \phi_{t} (q, p) (iii) marginalize the momenta, (q, p) -> q.  Each step in the
operation preserves pi(q) and so the entire transition preserves pi(q) and yields a
desired sample.  Note that T(q, p) can be almost anything and there is no Metropolis
correction here.

Now in practice we can’t do (ii) exactly and we have to approximate the flow with
a symplectic integrator.  This introduces error and pi(q) is no longer preserved
exactly.  Typically we fix this by treating the approximate flow as a proposal and
add a Metropolis correction, but this requires that the flow be reversible which
it is not.  To make the flow reversible we can do a few things — we can sample
the integration time from any distribution symmetric around zero or, if the
kinetic energy is symmetric with respect to p, we can add a momentum flip
at the end of the flow, (q, p) -> (q, -p).  Outside of NUTS people typically consider
a fixed integration time which leaves only the second option, hence the importance
of the symmetry of the kinetic energy.

What you’ve proposed is to sample from a distribution pi(p|q) = exp(-L(q, p))
that is not related to the kinetic energy.  Immediately this will cause a problem
because (i) will preserve only exp(-L) while (ii) preserves only exp(-T) and
the combined transition no longer has a stationary distribution.  So the exact
HMC algorithm doesn’t work.  We can still try to use this as a Metropolis-Hastings
proposal (although a poorly performing one) if we can make it reversible.
How we make it reversible depends on the choice of L(q, p), but it general
it will not be an easy problem.

Note that choosing a kinetic energy is a somewhat subtle problem.  Nominally
there are no constraints on T(q, p) which is usually a really bad sign — the
more the math constrains our options the less tuning we have to do and the
more robust the algorithm will be.  One way to introduce constraints is to
introduce more structure, such as a metric.  It turns out that a metric gives
a canonical family of kinetic energies with nice properties, and every member
of that family is symmetric because of the symmetry of the metric.  So
asymmetric kinetic energies are not only awkward to use they’re actually
really hard to motivate in the first place.

For all the gory details see http://arxiv.org/abs/1410.5110.

> ( Statement 1) If the kinetic energy equation comes from a distribution <tblatex-19.png> which is not a symmetric distribution, then thanks to the "Conservation of the Hamiltonian" property we'll still be able to accept the proposal with probability 1 if we are computing the Hamiltonian’s equations exactly.
>
> ( Statement 2) But if we are approximating the Hamilton’s equations by discretizing time (using leapfrog) then the acceptance probability [from <tblatex-22.png> to <tblatex-21.png>] won't be simply <tblatex-18.png>
>
> We would have to find <tblatex-17.png> for which <tblatex-16.png> will be the proposal values if we start from <tblatex-15.png>
>
> And, in this case, the acceptance probability will be: <tblatex-23.png>
>
> Are both  statements correct? If so, it seems that it's pretty difficult to find the value of <tblatex-17.png>...
>

messages.body_plain:
The answer I gave you before was right, but inefficient.

Reading Ruth King's paper made me think about the whole model
as an HMM and thus realize that the value chi[t] computed in
the Stan Manual's CJS model for the probability of being uncaptured (not sighted)
after time t was just the backward probability from the forward-backward
algorithm.   By analogy, I'm going to define a forward variable alpha[t]
that represents the probability of being unsighted up to time t-1 but being
alive at t.

Then, given first[i] as first sighting of i and last[i] as last sighting
of i, we can use the forward value up to first[i] and backward value back
to last[i] and condition everything in the middle knowing that all the x[i,t] = 1
(the individual can't die and come back to life between first[i] and last[i]).

So I'd probably write this as a likelihood function for y conditioned on
a whole bunch of things:

real
log_likelihood(int[] y,       // observations
               int first,     // first sighting time
               int last,      // last sighting time
               vector alpha,  // in study at first sighting
               vector chi,    // unsighted after last sighting
               vector phi,    // survive from t to t+1
               vector p) {    // sighted given alive
  real ll;
  ll <- alpha[first] + chi[last];
  for (t in first:(last-1))
    ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t]);
  for (t in first:last)
    ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(y[t], p[t]);
  return ll;
}

The first loop is that it survives from each point to the next
point between first and last (you don't know if you survive beyond
last, which is why phi[last] isn't included).  The second loop just
takes the sighting/capture probabilities for each point.

The first, last, and alpha values all get computed as in the previous model.
I'd define first and last as transformed data so as not to have to recompute.

Im assuming alpha and chi are defined on the log scale.

You can then define alpha and chi as locals in the model block, where
b[t] is chance of entering study at time t.

  alpha[1] <- log(b[1]);
  for (t in 2:T)
    alpha[t] <- log_sum_exp(alpha[t-1] + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t-1]),
                            b[t]);

The log_sum_exp is for the mixture of either being in the study at time t-1
and surviving to time to or entering the study at time t.

Moving on to the abundance study, you'll also have a bunch of individuals
who were never sighted.  So you have to increment the log density by the
probability of that, too.  Which is another calculation like the others,
because they can come into the study or exit the study, but at each point they
are in the study, they are unobserved.

I think that's it.  Let me know if you have more questions.

This is fun!  Especially when I don't have to debug it all.  You
really want to check all the boundary conditions in the above to make
sure they're right.

- Bob

When I was thinking about detailed balance the other day I made
up two examples which I found super helpful for understanding mixing.

I'm not sure why I haven't seen this before or maybe I have and just
didn't remember.

Consider a Markov chain with transition probabilities:

   A -> A : 0.4      B -> A : 0.4
   A -> B : 0.6      B -> B : 0.6

It's easy to see with this example that the stationary distribution
for a chain y drawn this way has

  Pr[y[t] = A] = 0.4
  Pr[y[t] = B] = 0.6

In fact, this Markov chain is really just a sequence of independent
draws because the chance of being in A at time t+1 doesn't depend on
which state you're in at time t.

Contrast that with transition probabilities:

  A -> A : 0.9      B -> A :  1/15
  A -> B : 0.1      B -> B : 14/15

This produces chains with the the same stationary distribution, but
it doesn't mix as well due to the autocorrelation.

The detailed balance condition is that the probability of being in
state A and moving to B is the same as being in B and moving to A.

  Pr[A] * Pr[A -> B] = Pr[B] * Pr[A -> B]

You can verify it for the above chains.

You can think of continuous versions of MCMC the same way --- you
just partition the space into two pieces, A and B, and look at probabilities
of transitioning between them (or generalize to more states).  It makes
much more sense (to me at least) than thinking about densities --- for
instance, it makes the Goodman and Weare ensemble sampler clearer as to
why it needs to do the Jacobian adjustment it does.

This is going on a slide or two for our upcoming class where I believe
I'm on the hook to do a day of Bayes and MCMC.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'd like to be able to export quantities used in the computation of the log-posterior without having to re-declare and re-compute them in the "generated quantities" part of a Stan model. After attentive perusal of the Stan manual, I saw no way to do this.

Could it be possible to add, for example, a keyword (e. g. "exported") to the declaration of the quantity ?

Nota Bene : I am aware of the possibility of declaring transformed parameters. But the interesting quantities might be function of other "uninteresting" quantities computed earlier in the model part. Including them in a "transformed parameter" part would export also those "uninteresting" quantities.

Possible applications : DIC, WAIC, mixtures of already-fitted models, etc...

What do you think ?

messages.subject: Non-linear hierarchical fit: First order compartment model in cross-over design
messages.subject_clean: Non-linear hierarchical fit: First order compartment model in cross-over design
messages.body_plain:
We have recorded hormone concentration time series from 17 subjects, each under 4 treatments in a cross-over design. See HFit.pdf for the raw data and a first order compartment model fit similar to SSfol in R-package nlme. Treatment em (1..4) for each of the coefficients is the parameter of interest:

y[n] <- D_1 * Ke_1 * Ka_1 * (exp(-Ke_1*minut) - exp(-Ka_1*minut)) / (Ka_1 - Ke_1);

A fit similar to that in 17.3 of ARM (treatment and airport flight simulator) gives reasonable results

lKe_1_emn <- lKe_1_em[emn]  + lKe_1_subj[subjn]; # and similar for the other parameters

but this does not reflect the nested structure of the design; I could not find a nested formulation that converges comparably.

Any ideas are welcome. The example files attached are self-contained, all data are in .Rdata

> 2015-04-06 4:48 GMT-03:00 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:
> I just simulated the data and found your problem.
> Your hierarchical prior parameters are vectors rather than
> scalars.  This will cause the model to not be identified
> and Stan will march all over the "posterior", whereas Gibbs
> will move in a random walk, making it seem like Gibbs is
> sampling from the posterior.
>
> There's a more thorough discussion in the problematic posteriors
> section of the manual with a very simple example involving normal
> location (mean) parameters.
>
> When I fix that problem and simulate data with N = 1000 and G=10,
> Stan recovers the simulated parameters within their 95% intervals
> in roughly 40 seconds using default settings.
>
> I'm attaching both my simulator and the revised model.
>
> - Bob
